title: The digestive system: what teeth, enzymes and gut microbes each do to your food

summary.text: A little saliva turns thick starch paste runny in ten minutes, but it does nothing to a thick gel of isabgol. Why? In this lesson you will race four pastes down a tilted plate to find what stops saliva working, time how fast your mouth makes saliva, and test whether chewing helps.
summary.art: A girl kneeling beside a big steel plate propped on two books, watching four blobs of white paste, one of which has run far down the plate, while her mother holds a ruler.

intro.hook: A cow lives on grass. If you ate only grass, you would starve. You and the cow both have teeth, a stomach and intestines. So what does the cow have that you do not have?
intro.text: Grass is mostly fibre, and no enzyme made by a cow or a human can cut fibre. An enzyme is a substance made by living cells that cuts one kind of food molecule. The cow keeps a huge store of microbes in her stomach, and the microbes cut the fibre. You keep microbes too, in your large intestine, but far fewer than she does. In this lesson you find what each part of your digestive system does to food. You find out why a crushed lump dissolves faster than a whole one, and what that means for chewing. You test what stops the enzyme in your saliva. You find a food that your saliva cannot change at all.
intro.art: A girl and a cow looking at each other over a low wall, the cow chewing grass and the girl holding a plate of rice and dal.

outcomes: I can name the organs of the digestive system in order, and say the job of each.
I can name the four kinds of teeth and the three layers of a tooth, and say what each does.
I can explain what an enzyme is, and why each enzyme cuts only one kind of food molecule.
I can explain, using my Run Test, how heat and acid stop the enzyme in saliva.
I can say which juice works on starch, protein and fat, and where each juice is added.
I can explain how digested food and water pass into the blood and reach every cell.
I can explain what gut microbes do with fibre, and why plant-eating animals need them most.
I can plan a fair test with a control, measure the result and explain what I found.

terms.meaning: The food tube from the mouth to the anus, with the organs that pour juices into it.
terms.example: The mouth, food pipe, stomach, small intestine and large intestine form the tube. The liver and the pancreas send juices in.
terms.art: A body outline with one tube from mouth to bottom in one colour, and the liver and pancreas beside it in another colour.

terms.meaning: A flat front tooth with a thin edge, used for cutting. A grown-up has eight incisors.
terms.example: Your incisors cut a neat curve out of a slice of apple.
terms.art: A close view of four upper front teeth biting into a slice of apple.

terms.meaning: A pointed tooth beside the incisors, used for gripping and tearing. People have four canines.
terms.example: You use a canine to tear a tough piece of roti or sugarcane.
terms.art: A child's smile with the four pointed teeth shaded, one at each corner of the upper and lower rows.

terms.meaning: The broad back teeth, with bumpy tops, used for crushing and grinding. Premolars sit in front of the molars.
terms.example: Your molars grind roasted chana into a paste.
terms.art: A side view of a lower jaw with the broad back teeth shaded and a chana being crushed between upper and lower molars.

terms.meaning: The white outer layer of a tooth. Enamel is the hardest substance in the body, and it has no living cells.
terms.example: A chip in the enamel never heals, because no cells are there to mend it.
terms.art: A tooth cut in half from top to bottom, with the thin white outer layer coloured and labelled.

terms.meaning: The two inner layers of a tooth. Dentine is the hard yellowish layer under the enamel. The pulp is the soft centre, with nerves and blood vessels.
terms.example: A tooth hurts when decay reaches the dentine, because the dentine passes signals to nerves in the pulp.
terms.art: A tooth cut in half showing three layers: white enamel, yellow dentine and a pink centre with fine red and blue lines.

terms.meaning: The watery juice made by three pairs of glands around the mouth. Saliva wets food, protects teeth and starts to digest starch.
terms.example: Your mouth makes about 1 litre of saliva every day.
terms.art: A side view of a head with three small glands marked near the ear, under the jaw and under the tongue.

terms.meaning: A small flap at the back of the throat that folds down over the windpipe when you swallow.
terms.example: The epiglottis keeps food out of the windpipe, unless you laugh while you swallow.
terms.art: A side view of a throat, with a flap folding down over the windpipe while a bite goes down the food pipe.

terms.meaning: A substance made by living cells that speeds up one kind of chemical change. A digestive enzyme cuts one kind of food molecule into smaller pieces.
terms.example: The enzyme in saliva cuts starch. It does nothing to protein, fat or fibre.
terms.art: A long chain of beads with a small shaped clamp fitted round one join, and the chain coming apart at that join.

terms.meaning: The enzyme that cuts starch into sugar. Saliva holds amylase, and so does the juice of the pancreas.
terms.example: Amylase in your saliva turns thick starch paste runny in the Run Test.
terms.art: A drop of saliva falling onto a chain of sugar units, with the chain breaking into pairs.

terms.meaning: A long chain of sugar units that plants make to store food. Rice, wheat, ragi and potato are rich in starch.
terms.example: One starch molecule can hold thousands of sugar units joined in a row.
terms.art: Grains of rice beside a zoom-in circle showing a long coiled chain of identical beads.

terms.meaning: The juice made by the stomach wall. Gastric juice holds hydrochloric acid and an enzyme called pepsin.
terms.example: A grown-up's stomach makes about 1.5 litres of gastric juice a day.
terms.art: A stomach cut open, with drops of juice coming out of tiny pits in its wall.

terms.meaning: The enzyme in gastric juice that starts to cut proteins. Pepsin works only in acid.
terms.example: Pepsin starts to cut the protein in dal, egg and paneer into shorter chains.
terms.art: A stomach with a folded protein chain inside, being cut into shorter pieces.

terms.meaning: A yellow-green liquid made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. Bile breaks fat into tiny droplets. Bile is not an enzyme.
terms.example: Bile breaks up the ghee on your rice so that an enzyme can reach the fat.
terms.art: A liver and a small green bag under it, with a thin tube leading into the first part of the small intestine.

terms.meaning: An organ that makes a juice for the body to use.
terms.example: The liver is the biggest gland in the body. It makes bile.
terms.art: A liver on the right side of a body outline, with a small green bag of bile beneath it.

terms.meaning: The juice made by the pancreas. It holds enzymes for starch, protein and fat, and a base that cancels stomach acid.
terms.example: Pancreatic juice finishes cutting the starch that saliva began to cut.
terms.art: A pancreas behind a stomach, with a thin tube carrying juice into the small intestine.

terms.meaning: Tiny finger-shaped bumps that cover the inside of the small intestine. Digested food passes through them into the blood. One of them is called a villus.
terms.example: Each villus is up to about 1 millimetre tall and has fine blood vessels inside.
terms.art: A zoom-in circle on the wall of the small intestine showing rows of tiny fingers, each with red and blue vessels inside.

terms.meaning: The passing of digested food and water through the wall of the intestine into the blood.
terms.example: Sugar from your rice is absorbed in the small intestine and reaches your muscles in the blood.
terms.art: Small dots crossing the wall of a villus into a blood vessel, with an arrow leading away to the body.

terms.meaning: The parts of plant food that human enzymes cannot cut. Most fibre is made of chains of sugar units.
terms.example: The skin of rajma, the strings in drumstick and the bran of wheat are rich in fibre.
terms.art: A plate with rajma, a drumstick piece, a guava and a whole-wheat roti.

terms.meaning: The bacteria and other tiny living beings who live in the food tube. Most of them live in the large intestine.
terms.example: A grown-up carries tens of trillions of gut microbes, weighing about 200 grams together.
terms.art: A zoom-in circle on the large intestine showing many tiny rod and ball shapes of different colours.

terms.meaning: The way microbes break down food without using oxygen. Fermentation makes acids and gases.
terms.example: Bacteria in your large intestine ferment fibre. Bacteria in a pot of milk ferment milk sugar and make curd.
terms.art: A pot of setting curd beside a drawing of a large intestine, with small bubbles in both.

terms.meaning: Lactose is the sugar in milk. Lactase is the enzyme in the small intestine that cuts lactose in two.
terms.example: A baby makes plenty of lactase. Most grown-ups in the world make much less.
terms.art: A steel tumbler of milk beside a pair of joined beads being cut apart.

terms.meaning: A heavy, sore or burning feeling in the belly after a meal.
terms.example: Eating very fast or eating food that has turned bad can give indigestion.
terms.art: A child holding a sore belly beside a plate of food left out overnight.

terms.meaning: The part of a fair test where the thing you are testing is left out. You compare everything else with the control.
terms.example: In the Run Test, the cup with water and no saliva is the control.
terms.art: Four small steel cups in a row, the first one marked with a tick and the word 'water'.

explanations.concept: The digestive system: one tube, many stations
explanations.definition: The digestive system breaks food into molecules small enough to pass into the blood, and sends out what cannot be used.
explanations.description: Food is made of molecules, which are particles far too small to see. Many food molecules are long chains. Starch is a chain of sugar units. A protein is a chain of amino acids. A fat is built from smaller units too. Only single units, or pairs of them, can cross the wall of the intestine. So the body must cut the chains. It does this along one tube, 5 to 9 metres long in a grown-up. The stations come in a fixed order. The mouth breaks and wets the food and starts on starch. The food pipe, or oesophagus, squeezes it down to the stomach. The stomach churns it with acid and starts on protein. The small intestine finishes the cutting and absorbs the pieces. The large intestine takes back water and houses the gut microbes. The rectum stores what is left, and it leaves by the anus. Two organs help from outside the tube. The liver sends in bile, and the pancreas sends in pancreatic juice.
examples: Food passes through the mouth, the food pipe, the stomach, the small intestine, the large intestine, the rectum and the anus, in that order.
Breaking by force is called mechanical digestion. Teeth and the stomach wall do it.
Cutting molecules is called chemical digestion. Enzymes do it.
Water, salt and vitamins are already small. They need no digesting.
explanations.art: A body outline with the food tube drawn as a line of seven labelled stations, like stops on a railway map.

explanations.concept: Teeth: four kinds, two sets and three layers
explanations.definition: Teeth are the hard tools of the mouth. Each kind of tooth has a shape that fits one job: cutting, tearing or grinding.
explanations.description: A grown-up has 32 teeth. Count one quarter of the mouth, from the middle to the back. There are 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars. Incisors cut. Canines grip and tear. Premolars and molars crush and grind. A small child has only 20 milk teeth, with no premolars. From about the age of six, milk teeth fall out and permanent teeth replace them. At six, the first permanent molars also come in behind the milk teeth. A child of ten usually has about 24 teeth, some milk and some permanent. The last four molars are called wisdom teeth. They usually come in during the late teens or early twenties, and in some people they never come. A tooth has three layers. The enamel on the outside is the hardest substance in the body. Under it is dentine, which is hard but living. In the centre is the pulp, with nerves and blood vessels. The root holds the tooth in the jaw bone. Enamel has no cells, so the body cannot mend it. Acid made by mouth bacteria from sugar slowly dissolves enamel. Chewing matters for digestion because small pieces give enzymes far more surface to work on. You can protect your enamel. Brush twice a day. Rinse your mouth with water after meals, and eat fewer sweets, because sugar is the food of the bacteria that make the acid. See a dentist if a tooth hurts, if gums bleed, or if you see a dark spot or a hole. A dentist can also find trouble before it hurts. Chew small mouthfuls, and do not talk or laugh with food in your mouth. At the back of the throat, the food pipe lies behind the windpipe, the tube that carries air to the lungs. When you swallow, a small flap called the epiglottis folds down over the top of the windpipe. Talking or laughing keeps the windpipe open, so a bit of food can slip in and make you cough. A cough pushes it back out. If a person cannot cough or breathe, call a grown-up at once.
examples: One quarter of a grown-up's mouth: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars. Four quarters make 32.
One quarter of a small child's mouth: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 molars. Four quarters make 20.
A cow has no upper front teeth. A tiger's canines are as long as your finger.
Sticky sweets that stay on the teeth are worse than a sweet that is gone quickly. Rinsing with water after a sweet helps to wash the sugar away.
explanations.art: A top view of a lower jaw with the teeth coloured by kind, beside a tooth cut in half to show enamel, dentine, pulp and root.

explanations.definition: Saliva is the juice of the mouth. It wets food, starts to digest starch and protects the teeth.
explanations.description: Three pairs of glands make saliva. One pair sits in front of the ears, one pair under the jaw and one pair under the tongue. Together they make about 1 litre a day. Saliva is 99 parts water in 100. The rest does most of the work. A slippery substance called mucus coats the food so that it slides down. The enzyme amylase starts to cut starch into sugar. Other substances in saliva kill some bacteria. Saliva also holds a weak base, which cancels the acid that mouth bacteria make. That is how saliva protects enamel between meals. At night the glands make very little saliva. So food left on the teeth at bedtime does the most harm. Your glands start before you eat. The sight, the smell or even the thought of food sends a signal from the brain to the glands. People do not all make the same amount of amylase. In 2007 a team led by George Perry counted the copies of the amylase gene in people from several groups around the world. The number of copies differed from person to person. Groups whose food is rich in starch had more copies on average.
examples: Chew plain rice for two minutes and it tastes faintly sweet, because amylase has made some sugar.
Iodine turns starch blue-black. Bread mixed with saliva for ten minutes turns a paler colour, because some of the starch has gone.
A dry mouth makes dry food very hard to swallow.
explanations.art: A side view of a head with the three pairs of saliva glands coloured, and small arrows showing saliva entering the mouth.

explanations.definition: An enzyme is a substance made by living cells that speeds up one kind of chemical change. Each digestive enzyme cuts one kind of food molecule.
explanations.description: An enzyme is a large molecule with a special shape. One part of it is a pocket. Only one kind of food molecule fits the pocket, as one key fits one lock. When the right molecule sits in the pocket, the enzyme cuts it at one join and lets the pieces go. The enzyme itself is not changed, so it can cut again and again. That is why a tiny amount of saliva can thin a whole spoonful of paste. An enzyme that cuts starch is called an amylase. An enzyme that cuts protein is called a protease. An enzyme that cuts fat is called a lipase. Many enzyme names end in '-ase'. The shape of an enzyme matters a great deal, because the shape decides what can fit in the pocket. Enzymes are proteins, and heat changes the shape of a protein for good. You have seen this when the clear part of an egg turns white in a hot pan. A strong acid also changes the shape. An enzyme with the wrong shape cannot hold its food molecule, so it stops working. In the Run Test you find this out with your own saliva.
examples: Amylase cuts starch. It cannot cut the protein in dal.
Pepsin cuts protein. It cannot cut starch.
No human enzyme fits the joins in cellulose, the fibre of plant cell walls.
Washing powders with enzymes use the same idea to cut food stains out of clothes.
explanations.art: Three differently shaped clamps, each fitted to its own kind of bead chain, with one clamp that does not fit a fourth chain.

explanations.concept: Every station keeps the conditions its enzymes need
explanations.definition: Each part of the food tube is kept at the acidity that suits the enzymes working there.
explanations.description: The whole tube is at body warmth, about 37 degrees Celsius. Digestive enzymes work fast at this warmth. The acidity changes from station to station. Scientists measure acidity on the pH scale. A pH of 7 is neutral, like pure water. Lower numbers are more acid, and higher numbers are more basic. The mouth is close to neutral, and amylase works well there. The stomach is strongly acid, with a pH of about 2. Amylase stops working in acid. Pepsin is the opposite. Pepsin works only in acid. So starch digestion stops in the stomach and protein digestion starts. A swallowed lump of food is not sour in the middle at first. The amylase inside the lump keeps working for some minutes, until the acid soaks in. When food leaves the stomach, the pancreas adds a base that cancels the acid. The small intestine is close to neutral again. Pepsin stops, and the enzymes of the pancreas take over.
examples: In the mouth, the acidity is about pH 7, which is close to neutral. This is where amylase works.
In the stomach, the acidity is about pH 2, which is strongly acid. Pepsin works there, and amylase stops.
In the small intestine, the acidity is about pH 7 again. The enzymes of the pancreas work there, and pepsin stops.
Lemon juice has a pH of about 2, which is why it can stand in for stomach acid in the Run Test.
explanations.art: A food tube drawn as a strip with three coloured zones, labelled mouth pH 7, stomach pH 2 and small intestine pH 7, with a different enzyme shape in each zone.

explanations.concept: The stomach: acid, pepsin and a wall that protects itself
explanations.definition: The stomach stores and churns food, kills many swallowed microbes with acid, and starts to digest protein.
explanations.description: The stomach wall has millions of tiny pits. Cells in the pits make hydrochloric acid, and other cells make pepsin. The acid does three jobs. It kills many of the microbes that come in with food. It loosens the folded shape of proteins. It also switches pepsin on. The cells release pepsin in a form that cannot cut anything. Only when it meets acid, out in the hollow of the stomach, does it become active. This keeps the cells that make pepsin safe from their own enzyme. The stomach wall is made of protein too. A thick coat of mucus, with a base in it, covers the wall and keeps the acid away. The cells of the lining are also replaced every few days. The stomach absorbs almost no food. After some hours of churning, it passes a thick liquid on to the small intestine, a spoonful or so at a time. In 1823 the English doctor William Prout showed that the acid in the stomach is hydrochloric acid.
examples: Acid alone does not digest a meal. It prepares protein for pepsin.
Pepsin cuts long protein chains into shorter chains. Other enzymes finish the job later.
A few kinds of bacteria can live in the stomach. One kind makes a base around themselves to cancel the acid.
explanations.art: A zoom-in on the stomach wall showing a pit, a thick layer of mucus over the cells, and drops of acid and enzyme rising into the hollow of the stomach.

explanations.concept: The small intestine: three juices finish the cutting
explanations.definition: In the small intestine, bile, pancreatic juice and the enzymes of the intestine wall cut food into units small enough to absorb.
explanations.description: The small intestine is 3 to 6 metres long in a grown-up, and most digestion happens here. Three juices work on the food. Bile comes from the liver. It breaks fat into tiny droplets, as dish soap does to grease. Bile is not an enzyme and cuts no molecules. Pancreatic juice comes from the pancreas. It holds amylase for starch, several proteases for protein and lipase for fat. It also holds the base that cancels stomach acid. The third set of enzymes sits on the surface of the villi. These enzymes make the last cuts. One of them cuts malt sugar into two units of glucose. Another cuts table sugar. Another, called lactase, cuts milk sugar. At the end, starch has become glucose. Protein has become single amino acids. Fat has become fatty acids and smaller parts. The pancreas releases its proteases switched off, as the stomach does with pepsin. They become active only inside the intestine. The liver is the biggest gland in the body. A gland is an organ that makes a juice for the body to use. The liver lies on the right side of the stomach, under the lower ribs. The pancreas is a gland too, but a much smaller one.
examples: Starch is cut by amylase, first in the mouth and then in the small intestine. The last cut, made on the villi, gives glucose.
Protein is cut first by pepsin in the stomach, and then by proteases in the small intestine. It ends up as single amino acids.
Fat is first broken into tiny droplets by bile. Then lipase cuts the fat in the small intestine.
A person whose gall bladder has been removed still makes bile. The bile drips in slowly, so very fatty meals are harder to digest.
explanations.art: The first part of a small intestine with two thin tubes entering it, one from the liver and gall bladder and one from the pancreas, and three kinds of chain being cut inside.

explanations.concept: Absorption: from the tube to every cell
explanations.definition: Absorption is the passing of digested food and water through the wall of the intestine into the blood.
explanations.description: The lining of the small intestine is folded and covered with villi. This gives it a surface of about 30 square metres. Each villus holds fine blood vessels. Glucose and amino acids pass through the wall of the villus into this blood. The blood goes first to the liver. The liver stores some glucose and makes many harmful substances safer. Then the blood flows to the heart, and the heart pumps it to every cell of the body. The cells use glucose for energy and amino acids for building. Fats take another route. They pass into fine tubes called lymph vessels and join the blood later, near the heart. Water is absorbed too. Textbooks say about 2 litres of water come in with food and drink each day. The body adds about 7 litres of juices. So about 9 litres enter the tube. The small intestine takes back most of it. The large intestine takes back most of the rest. Only about 100 millilitres leave the body in the faeces.
examples: A glucose molecule crosses a villus into the blood. The blood carries it to the liver, then to the heart, and then to a muscle in your leg.
A fat molecule crosses a villus into a lymph vessel. The lymph joins the blood later, and then the fat reaches a cell that stores or uses it.
Of 9 litres of water that enter the tube, the body takes back about 8.9 litres.
explanations.art: One villus drawn large, with dots passing into its blood vessel, and a long arrow leading to a liver, a heart and a leg muscle.

explanations.concept: Milk sugar: why many grown-ups cannot digest milk
explanations.definition: Lactose, the sugar in milk, can be absorbed only after the enzyme lactase cuts it in two. Most grown-ups make little lactase.
explanations.description: Every baby mammal lives on milk, and the baby's small intestine makes plenty of lactase. In most mammals, the body makes less and less lactase after the young stop drinking milk. Humans are the same. In about two in three grown-ups in the world, lactase falls to a low level after early childhood. When such a person drinks a lot of milk, the lactose is not cut. It passes on to the large intestine. The bacteria there ferment it and make gas and acids. This can cause a stomach ache and loose motions. It is not an illness. In 1965 doctors tested healthy grown-ups and found that low lactase was common. In 1981 Rakesh Tandon and his team tested healthy grown-ups in India. About two in three of the people from South India had low lactase. About one in four of the people from North India had it. Some groups of people keep making lactase all their lives. Their ancestors herded cattle, goats or camels, and this change spread among them in the last 10,000 years. Curd is easier to digest than milk. The curd bacteria have used up part of the lactose, and they carry lactase of their own.
examples: A person with low lactase can often drink a small tumbler of milk with no trouble, but not a large one.
Curd, buttermilk and hard cheese hold less lactose than milk.
Lactose-free milk has had lactase added at the dairy, so the cutting is already done.
explanations.art: A grandmother holding a small steel tumbler of milk in one hand and a bowl of curd rice in the other, with a small drawing of joined and cut sugar pairs above each.

explanations.concept: Fibre and gut microbes: the digesting you cannot do yourself
explanations.definition: Gut microbes are the bacteria and other tiny living beings in the food tube. They ferment the fibre that human enzymes cannot cut.
explanations.description: Fibre is made mostly of chains of sugar units, as starch is. The joins between the units are different. The human body makes only a few enzymes for cutting such chains, and none of them fits the joins in fibre. So fibre reaches the large intestine uncut. Tens of trillions of bacteria live there, of many kinds. Together they weigh about 200 grams. They make thousands of enzymes that the human body does not make. One kind of gut bacterium, called Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, has more than 100 enzymes for cutting sugar chains. The bacteria ferment the fibre and make small acids. The cells of the large intestine absorb these acids and get most of their own energy from them. A small part of a person's energy, up to about a tenth, comes this way. The bacteria also make vitamin K and some B vitamins. They take up space and food, so harmful microbes find it hard to settle. They make gases too, and that is normal. A baby gets their first gut microbes at birth, and more from milk and from the people around them. Human milk holds special sugars that the baby cannot digest. These sugars feed the baby's gut bacteria.
examples: Foods rich in fibre: rajma, chana, whole wheat, ragi, guava, greens and most vegetables.
Foods with almost no fibre: milk, egg, fish, meat, sugar and maida biscuits.
A meal of rajma makes more gas than a meal of white rice, because more of it reaches the bacteria.
A course of antibiotics kills many gut bacteria as well as harmful ones. The numbers usually recover over some weeks.
explanations.art: A large intestine with a zoom-in circle showing many kinds of bacteria around a strand of plant fibre, and small dots passing from them into the wall.

explanations.definition: Indigestion is a heavy, sore or burning feeling in the belly after eating. Most of the time it is mild, but a few signs mean a doctor must see the person.
explanations.description: Sometimes a meal sits badly. The belly feels heavy or sore, with burps or a sour taste. The causes are often plain. A very big or very oily meal takes the stomach a long time to empty. Eating very fast sends big lumps and swallowed air down. Spoiled food is worse. Cooked rice or dal left out all night in a hot kitchen grows bacteria, and some of them make poisons that cause vomiting and loose motions. So eat fresh food, keep it covered, and put leftovers in the fridge soon. Mild indigestion usually passes in a few hours. Many families give curd or buttermilk, which are gentle on the stomach and hold living bacteria. Scientists are still studying how much they help. If there are loose motions, drink ORS, the salt and sugar drink, to replace the water that is lost. Go to a doctor if the pain is strong or keeps coming back. Go too if vomiting will not stop, if there is blood in the vomit or the motion, or if a small child is very sleepy or has a very dry mouth.
examples: A heavy feeling after three helpings of a rich wedding meal usually passes with rest.
A child with loose motions after eating stale rice needs ORS and a visit to the doctor if it does not stop.
Chaas after lunch is a common way to settle a heavy stomach in many Indian homes.
explanations.art: A kitchen with a covered pot of fresh dal on the stove and a steel glass of chaas, beside a child holding a sore belly and a grown-up with a packet of ORS.
explanations.context: After the food tube and its microbes, this card shows what happens when digestion is upset. It tells what usually causes it, what helps at home and when a doctor is needed.

explanations.concept: Other animals: the same tube, with different lengths and chambers
explanations.definition: Humans and other animals with backbones share the same plan of food tube. What changes most with the kind of food is not the small intestine. It is the large intestine and the chambers where microbes work.
explanations.description: Meat is easy to digest, because an animal's own enzymes can cut it. Plants are hard to digest, because so much of a plant is fibre. No animal with a backbone is known to make an enzyme that cuts cellulose. So plant-eaters depend on microbes, and they give the microbes room and time. Many books say that plant-eaters simply have longer guts. In 2021 a team led by Maria Duque-Correa gathered published measurements from 519 kinds of mammal and tested this. They found that the old rule is weak. The small intestine follows body size more than food. Food changes the large intestine most, and the caecum, the side pouch where microbes work. Some plant-eaters also keep a huge chamber in the stomach. The measured lengths below are rounded, and they vary from animal to animal. A cat of about 2.5 kilograms, a meat-eater, has about 1.4 metres of intestine, and only about 25 centimetres of it is large intestine. A rabbit of about 3 kilograms, a plant-eater, has about 3.4 metres, and about 1.5 metres of it is large intestine, with a caecum about 40 centimetres long. A person of about 65 kilograms has about 8 metres of intestine, measured in people who had died, and about 1.6 metres of it is large intestine. Our caecum is small. A thin tube called the appendix hangs from it. Cattle of about 470 kilograms have about 51 metres of intestine, and about 10 metres of it is large intestine. A cow also has a stomach of four chambers. The first chamber, the rumen, holds many litres of grass, water and microbes. Teeth fit the food too. A cat's back teeth slice like scissors. A cow's back teeth are broad and flat for grinding. A crow has no teeth. A muscular part of her stomach, the gizzard, grinds the food.
examples: Cat, a meat-eater: about 1.4 metres of intestine, only about 25 centimetres of it large intestine, with sharp slicing teeth.
Human, who eats both: about 8 metres of intestine, about 1.6 metres of it large intestine, with four kinds of teeth.
Rabbit, a plant-eater: about 3.4 metres of intestine, about 1.5 metres of it large intestine, with a large caecum.
Cow, a plant-eater: about 51 metres of intestine, about 10 metres of it large intestine, with a four-chambered stomach.
explanations.art: Four animals in a row, a cat, a child, a rabbit and a cow, each with a coiled line beneath showing how long the intestines are, with the large intestine part drawn in a different colour.

explanations.concept: Did cooking shrink the human gut?
explanations.description: Humans have smaller teeth, weaker jaws and shorter intestines than other apes of our size. We also have much larger brains. In 1995 Leslie Aiello and Peter Wheeler pointed out that a gut and a brain both use a great deal of energy. They suggested that our ancestors could afford a large brain only because the gut became smaller. A smaller gut needs food that is easier to digest. The scientist Richard Wrangham argues that cooking provided it. Heat softens food, bursts starch grains and loosens proteins, so that enzymes work faster. Pounding and grinding help in the same way. On this idea, some of our digesting is done in the kitchen, before the first bite. Wrangham thinks cooking began almost 2 million years ago. The oldest fireplaces that everyone accepts are much younger than that. So scientists still argue about when cooking began and how much it changed our bodies.
examples: Cooked rice is digested far more easily than raw rice, because heat and water have burst the starch grains.
Idli batter is ground and fermented, so part of the breaking down is done before the meal.
Chimpanzees spend several hours a day chewing. People spend less than one hour.

perspectives.who: Richard Wrangham and those who agree
perspectives.explanation: Cooking gave more energy from the same food. Over a very long time, our ancestors' teeth and guts became smaller and their brains larger.
There is no firm sign of fire as old as the changes in teeth and gut. Cutting and pounding raw food, or eating more meat, could explain them.

explanations.art: An early human woman pounding roots with a stone beside a small fire, with a faint outline of a short food tube inside her body.

explanations.concept: Is the appendix a useless leftover?
explanations.description: The appendix is a thin tube, about as long as a finger, joined to the first part of the large intestine. People live well after a surgeon removes it. For over a century, many books called it a useless leftover from plant-eating ancestors. In 2007 William Parker's team in the United States proposed another idea. They suggested that the appendix is a safe store for helpful gut bacteria. After an illness has emptied the gut, bacteria from the appendix could fill it again. In 2013 Heather Smith and her team compared the guts of many kinds of mammal. They found that an appendix has appeared separately more than 30 times in the history of mammals. It has almost never been lost again. A part that keeps appearing is unlikely to be useless. But nobody has yet shown clearly what the appendix does in people.
examples: Rabbits, some monkeys and humans have an appendix. Dogs and cats do not.
In one study, people without an appendix got one serious gut infection again more often. Other studies did not find this.

perspectives.who: Scientists who think it is useful
perspectives.explanation: The appendix is rich in defence cells and holds a film of helpful bacteria. It has appeared many times in mammals, which suggests it does a job.
People without an appendix stay healthy. Until a clear job is shown in people, the safe store is only an idea.

explanations.art: The meeting point of the small and large intestine, with a thin finger-like tube hanging below it and a question mark beside it.

agreed.text: Digestion is done by enzymes, and each enzyme cuts one kind of food molecule.
agreed.evidence: In 1833 Anselme Payen and Jean-François Persoz separated a substance from sprouted barley that turned starch into sugar. In 1836 Theodor Schwann found pepsin in stomach juice. Hundreds of enzymes have since been separated and their shapes mapped.

agreed.text: Acid alone does not digest protein. The stomach needs pepsin, and pepsin needs acid.
agreed.evidence: Schwann showed that acid of the same strength as stomach juice hardly changed meat. Stomach juice dissolved it. Pepsin loses its power when the acid is cancelled.

agreed.text: The enzyme in saliva stops working in acid and after strong heating.
agreed.evidence: Chemists measure how fast amylase cuts starch at each pH and temperature. You can check it in the Run Test with your own saliva.

agreed.text: Human enzymes cannot cut fibre, and bacteria in the large intestine ferment it.
agreed.evidence: The human genome holds only a few genes for enzymes that cut sugar chains in food. One kind of gut bacterium holds more than 100. Animals raised with no gut microbes need more food to stay the same weight.

agreed.text: Most grown-ups in the world make little lactase, and this is normal.
agreed.evidence: Tests since 1965 on healthy grown-ups in many countries show low lactase in about two in three. A 1981 study found it in about two in three South Indians tested.

agreed.text: Plant-eating animals have larger spaces for microbes, in the large intestine, the caecum or an extra stomach chamber, where microbes cut the fibre.
agreed.evidence: Anatomists have measured the guts of hundreds of kinds of animal. In 2021 a study of 519 kinds of mammal found that the small intestine follows body size more than food, and that food changes the large intestine most. A cow's rumen holds a great deal, and scientists can take samples of its microbes.

challenging.who: A common belief, and the view of many scientists in the 1820s
challenging.for: Strong acid does dissolve many things, and the stomach is where we feel a meal.
challenging.against: Schwann showed in 1836 that acid alone hardly changes meat. The stomach's enzyme, pepsin, does the cutting. Most digestion happens later, in the small intestine, which is not acid at all.
challenging.context: This card is about what really breaks food down in the stomach.

challenging.claim: A grown-up who gets a stomach ache from milk is ill.
challenging.who: Many doctors in Europe and America before the 1960s
challenging.for: In their own countries, most grown-ups drank milk comfortably, so those who could not seemed unwell.
challenging.against: Tests around the world showed that low lactase is the usual state of a grown-up mammal. Making lactase for life is the newer and rarer condition.
challenging.context: This card is about whether digesting milk as a grown-up is normal.

challenging.claim: Fibre is useless, because we cannot digest it.
challenging.who: Many food scientists before the 1970s, who called fibre 'roughage'
challenging.for: No human enzyme cuts fibre, and it gives little energy.
challenging.against: Gut bacteria ferment fibre into acids that feed the cells of the large intestine. Fibre also holds water, which keeps the contents of the intestine soft and moving.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the part of food we cannot digest matters.

challenging.claim: One chewing rule is right for every food: chew each mouthful a very long time.
challenging.who: Horace Fletcher, an American writer on food, around 1900
challenging.for: Chewing well does break food small and mix it with saliva, and eating slowly helps people notice when they are full.
challenging.against: No test has shown that one rule suits every food. A banana is ready after a few chews, and a piece of coconut needs many more.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous rule for chewing.

challenging.claim: Cooking is what gave humans small guts and large brains.
challenging.who: Richard Wrangham, a scientist who studies apes and early humans
challenging.for: Cooked food gives more energy for less chewing and digesting. Human teeth, jaws and guts are small for an ape of our size.
challenging.against: The oldest agreed fireplaces are far younger than the changes in teeth and gut. Other causes, such as pounding food or eating meat, are possible.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the kitchen changed the human body.

challenging.claim: The appendix is a safe store for helpful bacteria.
challenging.who: William Parker and his team, from 2007
challenging.for: The appendix holds a film of helpful bacteria, and it has appeared more than 30 times among mammals.
challenging.against: People without an appendix live healthy lives. The job has not been shown clearly in people.
challenging.context: This card is about what the appendix might be for.

big_questions.q: Bacteria in your large intestine digest fibre that you cannot digest. So who digests your dinner: you, or you and the bacteria?
big_questions.hint: Think about what would reach your blood if the bacteria were not there.

big_questions.q: Your saliva worked on the starch paste in a cup, outside your body. Was that digestion?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the word needs: a body, or only an enzyme and its food?

big_questions.q: Cooking, grinding and fermenting all break food down before we eat it. Is a kitchen part of the human digestive system?
big_questions.hint: Compare a meal of raw rice grains with a meal of soft idli.

big_questions.q: A cow gives her microbes a warm home and grass. The microbes give her food. Who is working for whom?
big_questions.hint: Try telling the story from the microbes' side.

big_questions.q: Most grown-ups in the world cannot digest much milk. Who decides which kind of body is called normal?
big_questions.hint: Think about who wrote the first medical books on this, and where they lived.

big_questions.q: An enzyme fits one kind of molecule and no other. How could such an exact fit have come about with nobody designing it?
big_questions.hint: Think about living things changing a little in each generation over a very long time.

story.title: Paati's Stomach Page
story.note: Nila, Paati, Chithi and Saroja Athai are made up. These facts are real. Kumbakonam in Tamil Nadu is known for its filter coffee, called degree coffee, which is made with undiluted milk. In most grown-ups in the world, the small intestine makes little lactase, the enzyme that cuts milk sugar. A study in 1981 found this in about two in three South Indians tested. When curd sets, bacteria use up part of the milk sugar, and they carry lactase of their own. People differ in how much milk they can take, and many manage a small tumbler with no trouble. A stomach ache that keeps coming back needs a doctor.
text: Every time the family went to a wedding, Paati came home with a stomach ache.

"Hall food," she would say, pressing a hand under her ribs. "Too much oil. These cooks do not know when to stop." Then she would lie down with her knees drawn up, and nobody was allowed to talk about lunch.

Nila was ten, and she liked things to add up. This did not add up. At her cousin's wedding in Kumbakonam, Paati had eaten almost nothing from the leaf. She took a little rice, some rasam and one spoon of kootu. She waved the vadai away. Nila ate three vadai, and Nila felt fine.
On the train home, Nila opened her rough notebook and wrote at the top of a page: PAATI'S STOMACH. Under it she ruled three columns. What she ate. Where. Ache or no ache.
She kept the page for two weeks. Paati thought this was very funny. "Write that I ate your head," she said. But she answered every question.

The page grew. Idli and chutney, at home: no ache. Dosa at the bus stand hotel, shining with oil: no ache. That one surprised them both. Curd rice, at home, every single night: no ache. The wedding reception in Thanjavur: ache. Tea at Saroja Athai's house: ache. Bajji from the cart near the temple, fried in oil as black as the pan: no ache.

Nila read down the columns the way she checked a long sum. Oil did not fit. The dosa and the bajji had been swimming in oil. "Outside food" did not fit either. Saroja Athai's kitchen was cleaner than their own.
So what had Paati taken at the two weddings and at Saroja Athai's, and nowhere else?

Nila found her at the stove, making her evening coffee. Paati poured the dark decoction into her tumbler. Then she added milk, one spoon. "To change the colour," she always said. She had drunk it that way for forty years. Milk coffee, in Paati's opinion, was for children and guests.
"Paati, what coffee do they give at a wedding?"

"Degree coffee. What else, in Kumbakonam?" Paati looked pleased at the memory. "Thick milk, a little decoction, froth to the top. The boy comes down the row with the kettle and he does not ask how you take it. And when the coffee is that good, one does not say no to the second tumbler."
"And payasam?"
"Paal payasam. It was my own niece's wedding. Was I to refuse?"
"And Saroja Athai's tea?"
"Boiled in milk. Not one drop of water. She is very proud of it."

Nila went back to her page and wrote MILK at the bottom, and underlined it twice. Then she looked at the third line and crossed it out. Curd rice, every single night, no ache. Curd was milk. Paati ate a small hill of it.
She took the notebook to Chithi, her mother's younger sister, who tested milk at the dairy cooperative. Chithi read the whole page before she said anything. That was why Nila had chosen her.
"Your columns are right," said Chithi. "Milk gives her the ache, and curd does not. So what is the difference between milk and curd?"
"Curd is thick. And sour."
"Why is it sour?"
Nila set the curd every night, a spoon of old curd into warm milk. She knew this one. "The bacteria. They eat something in the milk and make it sour."

"They eat the sugar in the milk. By morning a good part of it is gone. Now listen. Milk sugar is too big to pass through the wall of the intestine. Something has to cut each piece in two first. A baby's intestine makes a cutter for it, an enzyme, because a baby lives on milk. In most people the intestine makes less and less of it as they grow up. Paati's makes hardly any now."
"So in her the milk sugar does not get cut."
"It goes straight through the small intestine to the large intestine. And who lives there?"
"More bacteria." Nila sat back. "They eat it there instead. And they make sour things. And gas?"
"A lot of gas, in a closed place. That is the ache."

Nila looked at her page. It was the same milk sugar, and nearly the same kind of eaters. In the curd pot, the bacteria did their eating on the kitchen shelf, the night before. In Paati, they did it afterwards, inside.
"Is Paati ill?"
"No. Most grown-ups in the world are like her. I am like her. The people who can drink a litre of milk at fifty are the unusual ones."
Nila told Paati all of it that evening. Paati listened with her chin up.

"A page in a rough notebook," she said. "Against forty years of knowing my own stomach." She thought for a while. "Then make me a wedding coffee. Here, in my own kitchen, in my own tumbler. No hall, no cook, no oil. If I ache, your page wins."

So on Sunday morning Nila made it, with more milk than decoction and froth to the top. Paati drank it slowly and said it was not bad for a first attempt. Then she asked for a second tumbler, to make the test fair.
Before noon she was lying down with her knees drawn up. "Write it down," she said crossly. "Go on. Write it down."
At the next wedding, in the month of Thai, the boy came down the row with his kettle. Paati put her hand flat over her tumbler.
"Decoction only," she said. "And one spoon of milk, to change the colour." She let the payasam pass. She took a second helping of curd rice.

On the train home she slept sitting up, with both hands in her lap. Nila took out the notebook. Under the last line of the page she wrote: Not the oil. Not the cook. Paati is not ill. She is short of one enzyme. Then she ruled a line under it, the way she did when a sum came out.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Paati blames the oil in wedding food for her stomach aches. Nila's page shows that oily food never gives her an ache, and milk does. But curd, which is made from milk, is safe. Lactose, the sugar in milk, must be cut in two by the enzyme lactase before it can be absorbed. Most grown-ups make little lactase, so the lactose reaches the bacteria of the large intestine, who ferment it and make gas. Curd bacteria have used up part of the lactose before the meal. One missing enzyme explains every line of the page.
ask: Why did oil not fit the facts on Nila's page?
Why does milk give some grown-ups a stomach ache when curd does not?
Paati asked for a second tumbler 'to make the test fair'. What did she mean?
Chithi said the people who can drink a litre of milk at fifty are the unusual ones. Why might that surprise many people?
What question about food and your own body could you answer with a page of three columns?

experiments.title: The Run Test: what stops saliva from digesting starch?
experiments.context: In this experiment you mix thick starch paste with water, with saliva, with heated saliva and with saliva and lemon juice. After ten minutes you race the four pastes down a tilted plate. The distance each paste runs shows whether its starch was cut.
experiments.question: Saliva holds an enzyme that cuts starch, and cut starch turns a thick paste runny. Does the enzyme still work after the saliva has been heated? Does it still work when lemon juice is added?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Four cups of thick paste get water, saliva, heated saliva, or saliva with lemon juice. Which pastes will turn runny, and which will stay thick? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: All four cups get the same paste from the same pot, 1 tablespoon each. Every cup gets half a teaspoon of a second liquid and half a teaspoon of a test liquid, so each has the same amount of liquid. All four are stirred 20 times and wait the same 10 minutes. All four blobs go on one plate and are tilted together, so the slope and the time are the same. The cup with water only is the control. It shows what the paste does with no saliva at all.
results_table: How far the blob ran in 1 minute (centimetres)

materials.item: the starch paste: 2 level tablespoons of cornflour stirred into 1 steel tumbler (200 millilitres) of cold water, then cooked. Rice flour or maida also works: use 3 level tablespoons
a small pan and the stove, used by a grown-up
small steel cups or katoris of the same size, labelled A, B, C and D
2 more small katoris, one for collecting saliva and one for heating it
a bowl of just-boiled water, deep enough to stand a katori in
half a lemon
teaspoons, a tablespoon and a tumbler of drinking water
a large steel plate or tray, about 30 centimetres across, and 2 or 3 thick books to lean it on
a ruler, a clock or phone timer, paper labels and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up cooks the paste and handles the just-boiled water. Each person uses only their own saliva. Nobody eats the pastes. Wash hands, cups and the plate with soap afterwards.

schedule.what: Cook and cool the paste. Collect saliva and heat one part of it. Mix four cups, wait 10 minutes, race the pastes down a tilted plate and measure.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Under it, write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how far each paste ran in 1 minute
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring a white paste in a small pan on a stove, with a spoonful held up to show that it is thick and holds its shape.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cooks the starch paste until it is thick. Spread it on a plate to cool.

setup.art: A child spitting into a small steel katori, and a second katori standing in a bowl of steaming water with a plate over it.
setup.caption: 2. Collect saliva and mix it with water. A grown-up heats one part of it for 5 minutes.

setup.art: Four small steel cups labelled A, B, C and D, each with a spoonful of white paste, and a child stirring one of them.
setup.caption: 3. Put paste in four cups. Add water, saliva, heated saliva, or saliva with lemon. Stir and wait 10 minutes.

setup.art: A large steel plate leaning on a stack of books, with four white blobs at the top edge, one of them running down in a long trail, and a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Put one blob from each cup at the top of a plate. Tilt the plate. After 1 minute, measure each trail.

flow.do: 1. Stir 2 level tablespoons of cornflour into 1 tumbler of cold water. 2. Heat it, stirring all the time, until it is thick and shiny. 3. Spread it on a steel plate to cool.
flow.say: I am cooking a paste that is almost pure starch. It must cool first, because hot paste would spoil the saliva.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cook the starch paste. Spread it on a plate. Let it cool.
flow.parent: A spoonful of the paste should hold its shape, like thick custard. If it is runny, cook it for two more minutes. It is ready to use when it no longer feels warm on your wrist, after about 15 minutes. Go on to the next two steps while it cools.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Run Test. A grown-up cooks a thick starch paste and leaves it to cool.

flow.do: 1. Explain the four cups. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason for each cup. 3. Write the guesses in the results table.
flow.say: Cup A gets water. Cup B gets saliva. Cup C gets saliva that has been heated. Cup D gets saliva and lemon juice. Which will turn runny?
flow.kid: Guess which cups will turn runny. Write your guess for each cup.

ask.q: Why do you think heated saliva will work, or will not work?
good: Heat might spoil the enzyme, the way cooking changes an egg.
Saliva is still saliva after heating, so it should work.
Warm things work faster, so it might work better.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. 'Warm things work faster' is a sensible idea, and the test will answer it.
flow.context: This is the second step of the Run Test. You guess which of four pastes will turn runny, before you mix anything.

flow.do: 1. Your child rinses their mouth and spits saliva into a katori until there is about 1 teaspoon. 2. Stir in 1 teaspoon of water. 3. Put half a teaspoon of this saliva mix into a second katori. 4. Stand that katori in just-boiled water for 5 minutes, covered.
flow.say: Rinse your mouth first. Now collect about a teaspoon of saliva. I will heat a small part of it.
flow.kid: Rinse your mouth. Spit into a katori until you have a teaspoon. A grown-up heats a little of it.
flow.parent: Collecting a teaspoon takes two or three minutes. The hot water must be just off the boil, so that the saliva in the katori gets very hot. Let the heated saliva cool for 3 minutes before you use it.
flow.context: In this step of the Run Test, you collect saliva, mix it with water, and heat one small part of it.

flow.do: 1. Put 1 tablespoon of cool paste in each cup. 2. Add half a teaspoon of lemon juice to D and half a teaspoon of water to A, B and C. Stir. 3. Add half a teaspoon of water to A, saliva mix to B and D, and heated saliva mix to C. 4. Stir each cup 20 times and note the time.
flow.say: Every cup gets the same paste and the same amount of liquid. The lemon goes into cup D first. Why must every cup get the same amount of liquid?
flow.kid: Put paste in four cups. Add the liquids as the table says. Stir each cup 20 times.
flow.parent: Use a clean spoon for each cup, so that no saliva is carried into cup A or cup C. Check that the paste is cool. Paste that is still hot will spoil the enzyme in every cup.

check.q: In the Run Test, cup A gets paste and water but no saliva. What is cup A for?
options: To show what paste does with no saliva
To use up the spare paste
To make the test take longer
check.why: Cup A is the control. Adding any liquid thins a paste a little. Cup A shows how much, so you can see what the saliva adds. If you chose 'spare paste', ask what you would compare cup B with.

flow.context: In this step of the Run Test, you mix the four cups: water, saliva, heated saliva, and saliva with lemon juice.

flow.do: 1. Leave the cups for 10 minutes. 2. Lean the big plate flat on the table, ready, with the books beside it. 3. After 5 minutes, let your child stir each cup once and say what they feel.
flow.say: The cups need ten minutes. Stir each one once with its own spoon. Does any cup feel different already?
flow.kid: Wait ten minutes. After five minutes, stir each cup once. Does any cup feel different?
flow.parent: Cup B usually feels thinner within two or three minutes. Let your child notice it without your saying why.
flow.context: In this step of the Run Test, the four cups stand for 10 minutes while the saliva works.

flow.do: 1. Put half a teaspoon from each cup near one edge of the flat plate. Set them in a row, in the order A, B, C, D. 2. Lift that edge onto the books in one smooth move. 3. After 1 minute, measure how far each blob has run.
flow.say: All four blobs start on one line. I will tilt the plate once, so that all four get the same slope. Measure each trail after one minute.
flow.kid: Put four blobs in a row on the plate. Tilt the plate. After one minute, measure each trail.
flow.parent: The top edge should be about 10 centimetres higher than the bottom edge. A runny paste reaches the bottom in seconds. If so, write 'ran off' and the length of the plate. The thick pastes may creep 1 to 3 centimetres.
flow.context: In this step of the Run Test, you race the four pastes down a tilted plate and measure how far each one runs.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Only then, read the explanation card on enzymes.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Which pastes ran, and which stayed thick?
good: Only the paste with plain saliva ran far.
The heated saliva and the lemon cups stayed thick, like the water cup.

ask.q: What does cup D tell you about saliva in the stomach?
good: The stomach is acid, like lemon juice.
So the enzyme in saliva stops working in the stomach.

flow.parent: The usual result: B runs far, and A, C and D stay thick. Cup D sometimes runs a little further than A, because the enzyme worked for a moment before the acid reached it. If nothing ran, the paste was probably still warm when the saliva went in.
flow.think: The lemon juice might have changed the paste by itself. What fifth cup would you add to check that?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Run Test. You compare the four distances and explain them.

experiments.title: Starch or Fibre: can saliva thin every thick food?
experiments.context: In the Run Test, saliva turned thick starch paste runny. In this experiment you try the same saliva on a thick gel made of fibre. It shows whether the enzyme in saliva cuts every chain of sugar units, or only starch.
experiments.question: Starch paste and isabgol gel are both thick, and both are made of long chains of sugar units. Saliva thins the starch paste. Does saliva thin the fibre gel too?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will add saliva to thick starch paste and to thick fibre gel. Will the fibre gel turn runny, as the starch paste does? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: There are four cups. Starch paste gets water in one cup and saliva in another. Fibre gel gets water in one cup and saliva in another. Every cup holds 1 tablespoon of paste or gel and half a teaspoon of liquid. Every cup is stirred 20 times and waits 10 minutes. Each food has its own water cup as a control, so you compare starch with starch and gel with gel.
results_table: How far the blob ran in 1 minute (centimetres)

materials.item: 4 tablespoons of cool starch paste, left from the Run Test or freshly cooked by a grown-up

the fibre gel: 2 level teaspoons of isabgol husk stirred into half a steel tumbler (100 millilitres) of water and left for 15 minutes. With no isabgol, slice 4 bhindi into 4 tablespoons of water, leave for 30 minutes, and use the slimy liquid
small steel cups or katoris of the same size, labelled 1 to 4
a katori for collecting saliva, teaspoons, a tablespoon and drinking water
a large steel plate or tray, 2 or 3 thick books, a ruler and a timer

experiments.safety: Each person uses only their own saliva. Nobody eats the pastes or gels. Wash hands, cups and the plate with soap afterwards.

schedule.what: Make the fibre gel. Mix four cups, wait 10 minutes, race the blobs down a tilted plate and measure.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Then write one sentence that starts 'The enzyme in saliva can cut' and one that starts 'It cannot cut'.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how far each blob ran in 1 minute
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child stirring pale husk into a steel tumbler of water, with a packet of isabgol beside it, and the same tumbler shown later full of thick clear gel.
setup.caption: 1. Stir isabgol husk into water. Wait 15 minutes until it is a thick gel.

setup.art: Four small steel cups in two pairs, one pair holding white paste and one pair holding clear gel, with a spoon in each.
setup.caption: 2. Set up four cups: starch with water, starch with saliva, gel with water, gel with saliva.

setup.art: A large steel plate leaning on books with four blobs at the top, the second one running far down and the other three staying near the top.
setup.caption: 3. After 10 minutes, race the four blobs down a tilted plate. Measure each trail after 1 minute.

flow.do: 1. Recall the Run Test, where saliva turned the starch paste runny. 2. Show the isabgol husk and say that it is plant fibre. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: In the Run Test, saliva made thick starch paste runny. This husk is plant fibre, and it also makes a thick gel. Will saliva thin the gel too?
flow.kid: Guess if saliva will thin the fibre gel. Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think saliva will thin the gel, or will not?
good: Saliva digests food, and this is food, so it should.
The enzyme may fit only starch, so it may not.
Both are thick, so saliva should thin both.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Stir the husk into the water now, because the gel needs 15 minutes to thicken.
flow.context: This is the first step of Starch or Fibre. You guess whether saliva can thin a fibre gel as it thins starch paste.

flow.do: 1. Your child rinses their mouth and collects about half a teaspoon of saliva. 2. Stir in half a teaspoon of water. 3. Put 1 tablespoon of starch paste in cups 1 and 2, and 1 tablespoon of gel in cups 3 and 4. 4. Add half a teaspoon of water to cups 1 and 3, and saliva mix to cups 2 and 4. Stir each 20 times.
flow.say: Each thick food gets one cup with water and one cup with saliva. Which two cups are the controls?
flow.kid: Collect some saliva. Set up the four cups. Add water to two and saliva to two. Stir each 20 times.
flow.parent: The gel should be about as thick as the starch paste. If it is runny, stir in another half teaspoon of husk and wait 5 minutes. Use a clean spoon for each cup.

check.q: In Starch or Fibre, why does the fibre gel get its own cup with water?
options: To compare gel with gel
Because the gel needs more water
To make four cups for the plate
check.why: The gel and the paste do not run the same way to begin with. So the gel with saliva must be compared with the gel with water. If you chose 'more water', check the table: every cup gets the same half teaspoon.

flow.context: In this step of Starch or Fibre, you set up four cups: starch paste and fibre gel, each with water and with saliva.

flow.do: 1. Wait 10 minutes. 2. Put half a teaspoon from each cup in a row near one edge of the flat plate. 3. Lift that edge onto the books. 4. After 1 minute, measure each trail.
flow.say: Ten minutes are up. Put the four blobs on one line and tilt the plate once. Measure each trail after one minute.
flow.kid: Wait ten minutes. Put four blobs in a row. Tilt the plate. Measure each trail.
flow.parent: The starch with saliva runs far. The two gel blobs should run about the same distance as each other. A gel blob may slide as one lump. Measure to its front edge.
flow.context: In this step of Starch or Fibre, you race the four blobs down a tilted plate and measure them.

flow.do: 1. Compare cup 1 with cup 2, and cup 3 with cup 4. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Then read the explanation card on fibre and gut microbes.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: What happens to fibre that no enzyme of yours can cut?
good: It travels on to the large intestine.
The bacteria there cut it.
Some of it leaves the body.

flow.parent: The usual result: saliva changes the starch and leaves the gel as it was. The enzyme fits starch and nothing else. If the two gel blobs differ by a centimetre or two, that is within what two blobs of the same gel would do.
flow.think: A cow eats almost nothing but fibre. Where must her fibre be cut, and by whom?
flow.context: This is the last step of Starch or Fibre. You compare the pairs of cups and explain what the enzyme in saliva can and cannot cut.

experiments.title: Listen to a Gut: is the food tube busier before lunch or after?
experiments.context: In this experiment you listen to a family member's belly with your ear and count the gurgles in three minutes. You do it just before lunch and again 20 minutes after lunch. The gurgles are made by the muscles of the stomach and intestines moving food, juice and gas.
experiments.question: The stomach and intestines squeeze and mix their contents, and this makes sounds. Does a belly make more sounds just before lunch, or 20 minutes after lunch?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will count belly sounds for three minutes before lunch and for three minutes after lunch. When will you count more? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Listen to the same person both times, lying on their back on the same mat. Put your ear on the same spot, just below and to the right of the navel. Count for exactly 3 minutes each time, in a quiet room with the fan off if you can. One count is not much to go on. So swap places and count the other person's belly too.
results_table: Sounds in 3 minutes, 20 minutes after lunch

materials.item: a family member who agrees to be listened to
a mat or a bed, in a quiet room
a phone timer or a clock
a cardboard tube from a kitchen roll, or a sheet of chart paper rolled into a tube. Your ear alone also works
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Ask before you listen, and listen over a thin shirt. Rest your ear or the tube gently. Do not press on a full stomach.

schedule.what: Guess. Count belly sounds for 3 minutes before lunch. Count again 20 minutes after lunch. Swap places each time. Compare the counts.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table for both people. Write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you heard, and why you think it happened.

setup.art: A mother lying on her back on a floor mat, and her daughter kneeling beside her with one ear on a cardboard tube that rests on the mother's belly.
setup.caption: 1. Before lunch, listen to a belly for 3 minutes. Make a tally mark for every gurgle.

setup.art: The same two people at a table finishing a meal of rice, sambar and vegetables, with a clock on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Eat lunch. Wait 20 minutes.

setup.art: The daughter listening to her mother's belly again in the same place, with a notebook showing two rows of tally marks.
setup.caption: 3. Listen again for 3 minutes on the same spot. Compare the two counts.

flow.do: 1. Explain the test. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write both in the notebook.
flow.say: We will count the sounds a belly makes, before lunch and after lunch. When do you think it will make more sounds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess when there will be more belly sounds. Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think there will be more sounds before lunch, or after?
good: A hungry stomach growls, so before.
After lunch there is food to mix, so after.
The gut works all the time, so about the same.

flow.parent: All three guesses are reasonable, and real bellies differ. Do not say which is right.
flow.context: This is the first step of Listen to a Gut. You guess when a belly makes more sounds, before lunch or after.

flow.do: 1. Just before lunch, one person lies on their back. 2. The other rests an ear or a tube just below and to the right of the navel. 3. Count every gurgle, rumble or squeak for 3 minutes. 4. Swap places and count again.
flow.say: Lie still and breathe quietly. I will start the timer. Make a tally mark for every sound you hear, loud or soft.
flow.kid: Put your ear on the belly, below the navel. Count every sound for three minutes. Then swap.
flow.parent: Long quiet gaps are normal before a meal. A count of anything from 0 to 20 in three minutes is possible. A long rolling growl counts as one sound.
flow.context: In this step of Listen to a Gut, you count the sounds of a belly for 3 minutes just before lunch.

flow.do: 1. Eat lunch and note the time you finish. 2. After 20 minutes, listen again on the same spot for 3 minutes. 3. Swap places and count again.
flow.say: Twenty minutes have passed since lunch. Listen on the same spot as before. Count for three minutes.
flow.kid: Wait twenty minutes after lunch. Listen on the same spot. Count for three minutes. Then swap.
flow.wait: Do this 20 minutes after lunch on the same day
flow.parent: Most people hear more sounds after the meal, often a soft, steady gurgling. Some people hear the loudest sounds before lunch. Write down what you really hear.

check.q: In Listen to a Gut, what makes the sounds you hear in a belly?
options: Gut muscles moving food, juice and gas
The heart pumping blood
Teeth still chewing the food
check.why: The walls of the stomach and intestines are muscle. When they squeeze liquid and gas along, it gurgles. If you chose the heart, listen higher up on the chest: a heartbeat is a steady thud, not a gurgle.

flow.context: In this step of Listen to a Gut, you count the sounds of the same belly 20 minutes after lunch.

flow.do: 1. Put the four counts side by side. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they heard, and why it happened. 3. Then explain the cleaning wave of an empty gut.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you heard, and why you think it happened. Was the gut ever completely silent?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you heard. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Does the gut stop working when it is empty?
good: No, it still made some sounds before lunch.
It moves even when there is no meal to digest.

flow.parent: After a meal, the stomach and small intestine mix the food steadily, so most people hear more sounds. An empty gut is not idle. About every 90 to 120 minutes, a strong wave of squeezing sweeps from the stomach along the small intestine and clears out leftovers. That wave is one cause of a growling stomach. If your two bellies gave opposite results, say so in your record. Two people are too few to settle the question.
flow.context: This is the last step of Listen to a Gut. You compare the counts from before and after lunch, and explain them.

activities.title: Mouth Waters: how fast do your saliva glands wake up?
activities.context: This is a short activity to try before you learn how saliva works. You will find out if your mouth makes saliva before any food arrives. You time how long a dry lip takes to turn wet, first at rest and then while you look at and smell a cut lemon.

materials.item: a lemon cut in half
clean tissues
a clock or phone timer with seconds
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Do not taste the lemon in this activity. Wash your hands after you touch it.
activities.record: Write the two times in seconds. Then write one sentence about what you think made the difference.

setup.art: A child sitting still and dabbing the inside of her lower lip with a clean tissue, a timer on the table in front of her.
setup.caption: 1. Dry the inside of your lower lip with a tissue. Time how long it takes to shine again.

setup.art: The same child holding half a lemon under her nose, with a second tissue in her other hand.
setup.caption: 2. Smell and look at a cut lemon. Dry your lip again and time it.

setup.art: A notebook page with two lines of times written in seconds and a short sentence under them.
setup.caption: 3. Write both times. Write what you think made the difference.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess whether their mouth makes more saliva when it only sees and smells food. 2. Ask for the reason. 3. Write both in the notebook.
flow.say: Do you think your mouth makes saliva before any food arrives?
flow.kid: Guess if your mouth makes saliva before food arrives. Write your guess.

ask.q: Why might a mouth make saliva before any food arrives?
good: It gets ready for the food.
It has smelled the food, so it starts early.
It does not wait, and it just keeps making saliva.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The test will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Mouth Waters. You guess whether the saliva glands start working before food arrives.

flow.do: 1. Sit still, with the mouth closed for 10 seconds. 2. Wipe the inside of the lower lip dry with a clean tissue. 3. Start the timer. 4. Stop it when tiny drops or a shine show on the lip, and look in a mirror if you wish.
flow.say: Wipe your lip dry. Start the timer now. Stop it the moment you see a shine of saliva on your lip.
flow.kid: Dry your lower lip with a tissue. Start the timer. Stop when it shines again.
flow.parent: Your child may need a mirror to see the shine. The first time is usually 20 to 60 seconds. Write down whatever you see.
flow.context: In this step of Mouth Waters, you time how long a dry lip takes to shine again, while you do nothing special.

flow.do: 1. Hold the cut lemon about 5 centimetres under the nose and look at it. 2. Wipe the lip dry with a new tissue. 3. Start the timer and stop it when the lip shines. 4. Write the time.
flow.say: Smell the cut lemon and look at it. Do not taste it. Wipe your lip dry and time it again.
flow.kid: Smell and look at the cut lemon. Dry your lip. Time it again. Do not taste.
flow.parent: Many children feel their mouth water within a few seconds. The lip may shine sooner than at rest, but one try is not enough to be sure. Try twice at rest and twice with the lemon if you have time.

check.q: In Mouth Waters, what happens to saliva when you only smell a lemon?
options: The glands may start before any food arrives
The glands wait until you swallow
The glands stop completely
check.why: Signals from the nose and eyes reach the brain, and the brain tells the glands to start. If you chose 'wait until you swallow', check your two times again.

flow.context: In this step of Mouth Waters, you time the same dry lip again while you look at and smell a cut lemon.

flow.do: 1. Compare the two times. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. What would a quick mouthful of saliva do for a dry bite of roti?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.
flow.parent: The glands are switched on by the brain, and the sight and smell of food are enough. This is why saliva is already there when the first bite arrives. The next two experiments show what that saliva does.
flow.context: This is the last step of Mouth Waters. You compare the two times and say why your mouth made saliva before eating.

activities.title: Whole or Crushed: why does chewing help the enzymes?
activities.context: In this activity you dissolve the same amount of kalkandu, which is rock sugar, as one whole lump, in small pieces and as powder. Enzymes work on the outside of food in the same way that water works on the outside of the lump. You will find out why chewing your food well helps.

materials.item: 3 lumps of kalkandu (rock sugar) of about the same size, each about the size of a peanut. Big crystals of ordinary sugar also work
a clean cloth and a rolling pin, or the base of a steel tumbler, for crushing
3 small steel katoris or glasses of the same size, labelled 1, 2 and 3
tap water at room temperature, about 100 millilitres in each katori
3 spoons, a clock or phone timer, a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the crushing. Do not taste the sugar water, because the katoris may not be clean enough for tasting.
activities.record: Write the time that each lump took to disappear. Then write which one dissolved first and why you think so.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: seconds for the sugar to vanish
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A cloth folded over a lump of rock sugar on a board, and a child's hand pressing a steel tumbler down on it while a parent holds the cloth still.
setup.caption: 1. Crush one lump into powder in a cloth. Break a second lump into four pieces. Keep the third whole.

setup.art: Three small steel katoris in a row, each half full of water, with a whole lump, four pieces and a heap of powder in front of them.
setup.caption: 2. Put 100 millilitres of water in each katori, with the three sugars ready beside them.

setup.art: A child dropping the sugar into all three katoris at the same moment, with a spoon in each katori and a timer showing.
setup.caption: 3. Drop all three in together. Stir each one once every second. Note when each one has vanished.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess which will vanish first and why. 2. Ask how much faster they expect. 3. Write both guesses in the notebook.
flow.say: The same amount of sugar goes in each katori, as one lump, as four pieces and as powder. Which vanishes first?
flow.kid: Guess which sugar will vanish first. Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think that one will vanish first?
good: Powder has more of its outside showing to the water.
Small bits are easier to break up.
The big lump has to be eaten away from the outside.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Crush one lump now, with the cloth held down firmly, while your child writes.
flow.context: This is the first step of Whole or Crushed. You guess which form of sugar will dissolve first.

flow.do: 1. Wrap one lump in a cloth. 2. Crush it to a fine powder with the base of a tumbler. 3. Wrap a second lump in the cloth and crack it into four pieces. 4. Keep the third lump whole.
flow.say: I will crush one lump to powder and break one into four pieces. The third stays whole. Is there still the same amount of sugar in each?
flow.kid: A grown-up crushes one lump and cracks one into four. The third stays whole.
