flow.parent: Brush every grain of powder out of the cloth into katori 3. Powder left in the cloth makes katori 3 look unfairly quick.
flow.context: In this step of Whole or Crushed, a grown-up crushes one lump of sugar, breaks one into four and keeps one whole.

flow.do: 1. Pour 100 millilitres of room-temperature water into each katori. 2. Drop the three sugars in at the same moment. 3. Stir each katori once every second. 4. Write the time when each one has completely vanished.
flow.say: Drop all three in together and start the timer. Stir each katori once every second, in the same way. Tell me the moment each one has vanished.
flow.kid: Drop all three in together. Stir once each second. Write when each one has gone.
flow.parent: The powder usually vanishes in under a minute. The whole lump can take several minutes, so stop at 8 minutes and write 'not yet'. A second person can help by watching one katori each. Stir in the same way every time, because stirring changes the speed.

check.q: In Whole or Crushed, why must all three katoris get the same amount of water and the same stirring?
options: So that only the size of the pieces differs
So that the water lasts longer
So that all three finish together
check.why: A fair test changes one thing only. Here it is the size of the pieces. If you chose 'finish together', that would make the result meaningless.

flow.context: In this step of Whole or Crushed, you drop the three sugars into water together and time how long each takes to vanish.

flow.do: 1. Compare the three times. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Then explain surface and chewing.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. A swallowed lump of food is like the whole sugar lump.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: What does chewing do for the enzymes in your mouth?
good: It gives them more of the food's outside to work on.
It breaks big lumps into small bits.
It is like crushing the sugar.

flow.parent: Water, like an enzyme, can only work on the outside of a piece. Cutting a piece into four, or into powder, makes much more outside. Chewing does the same to food. It does not make the food more nutritious. It makes digestion faster. One chewing rule does not suit every food, as the Fletcher card in the lesson shows.
flow.think: A cube of 2 centimetres is cut into eight cubes of 1 centimetre. Has the amount of food changed? Has the amount of outside changed?
flow.context: This is the last step of Whole or Crushed. You compare the three times and say why chewing helps digestion.

activities.title: The Gut Ladder: string lengths for a cat, a person, a rabbit and a cow
activities.context: In this activity you cut a paper strip for the real intestine length of a cat, a person, a rabbit and a cow, measured by scientists. You colour the large intestine part. The strips show that the biggest animal has the longest gut, and that food changes the large intestine most.

materials.item: old newspaper or a roll of string, about 7 metres in all
a ruler or a metre tape
scissors, used by a grown-up
sticky tape and a marker pen
a red marker pen, for the large intestine part
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Fill in a table of four animals: what each one eats, its weight, and the length of your whole strip and of the large intestine part.

example_chart.title: Intestine length from measured animals, rounded. The strips are cut at 1 centimetre of strip for every 10 centimetres of real intestine
example_chart.note: Source: measurements collected by Duque-Correa and others (2021), from a wild cat, a domestic rabbit, people who had died and cattle. Real animals vary a lot, so treat the numbers as about right. The scientists also found that the rule 'plant-eaters have longer guts' is weak.

setup.art: Four paper strips of different lengths laid side by side on a floor, labelled cat, human, rabbit and cow, with the cow's strip running off the end of the picture.
setup.caption: 1. Cut one strip for each animal, at 1 centimetre of strip for every 10 centimetres of real intestine.

setup.art: A child laying a long string along a hallway floor, with a marker note beside it saying 'cow, 510 cm, last 100 cm red'.
setup.caption: 2. Colour the last part of each strip red, the large intestine. Lay the strips out side by side.

setup.art: A table with four rows drawn in a notebook, and a pencil pointing to the cow's row.
setup.caption: 3. Fill in the table. Compare the cat and the rabbit, who weigh about the same.

flow.do: 1. Read out the four animals: cat, human, rabbit, cow. 2. Ask your child to put them in order from the shortest gut to the longest, and give a reason. 3. Write the order down.
flow.say: Here are four animals: a cat, a person, a rabbit and a cow. Put them in order, from the shortest gut to the longest. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put a cat, a person, a rabbit and a cow in order. Shortest gut first. Why?

ask.q: What made you put that animal last?
good: A cow is the biggest animal.
A cow eats only grass.
Plants are harder to digest.

flow.parent: Do not correct the order. Most children guess that size decides the order, and for the whole intestine they are right. The strips will also show what food changes.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Gut Ladder. You guess the order of the guts of a cat, a person, a rabbit and a cow.

flow.do: 1. Cut the strips at 1 centimetre of strip for each 10 centimetres of real intestine: cat 14 centimetres, rabbit 34, human 80 and cow 510. 2. Join strips of newspaper with tape, to make the long ones. 3. Colour the last part of each strip red (or stick red paper on it), for the large intestine: cat 2.5 centimetres, rabbit 15, human 16 and cow 100.
flow.say: Scientists measured real animals. A cat's intestine is about 1.4 metres, a rabbit's about 3.4, a person's about 8 and a cow's about 51. We cut one centimetre of strip for every 10 centimetres of real gut. Work out each strip with me.
flow.kid: Cut the strips: cat 14 centimetres, rabbit 34, person 80, cow 510. Colour the large intestine red.
flow.parent: The cow's strip is 5 metres and 10 centimetres, so you need a hallway or a balcony. A string works as well as paper. Your child can do the sums, and you do the cutting. The figures are rounded from published measurements, and real animals vary.
flow.context: In this step of The Gut Ladder, a grown-up cuts a body strip and a gut strip for each animal.

flow.do: 1. Lay the four gut strips side by side. 2. Ask your child to compare the animals that eat plants with the animal that eats other animals.
flow.say: Look at the four strips. Which is longest? Now look at the red parts. Compare the cat and the rabbit, who weigh about the same.
flow.kid: Lay out the four strips. Find the longest. Look at the red parts of the cat and the rabbit.

ask.q: The cat and the rabbit weigh about the same. Which part of their strips is most different?
good: The red part of the rabbit's strip is much longer.
The rabbit's red part is nearly half of its strip.
The cat's red part is small.

check.q: In The Gut Ladder, the cat and the rabbit weigh about the same. Which part of their guts differs most?
options: The large intestine, the red part, is much longer in the rabbit
The small intestine is ten times longer in the rabbit
The cat's whole intestine is longer than the rabbit's
check.why: The rabbit's large intestine is about six times as long as the cat's, and her whole intestine is about 2 times as long. Microbes work in the large intestine and the caecum. If you chose the small intestine, look again: the rabbit's is only a little longer than the cat's.

flow.context: In this step of The Gut Ladder, you lay the four strips side by side and compare the cat and the rabbit, who weigh about the same.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 2. Ask where on the rabbit's strip the microbes live. 3. Read the explanation card on other animals.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Which of your four animals needs its microbes the most?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.
flow.parent: The longest strip belongs to the biggest animal, because body size sets most of the length. Scientists used to teach that plant-eaters simply have longer guts. In 2021 a team that gathered measurements from 519 kinds of mammal found this rule weak. Food changes the large intestine most, and the small intestine follows body size more. The cat and the rabbit are the fair pair, because they weigh about the same. The rabbit's microbes live mostly in the caecum, a large side pouch at the start of the large intestine, and in the rest of the large intestine. The cow's microbes live mostly in her rumen, the first chamber of her stomach, which is not on these strips. Each strip stands for a few animals only: a wild cat for the cat, a domestic rabbit, people who had died, and cattle. Real animals vary a lot, so say 'about'.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Gut Ladder. You say what the long guts have in common and why.

activities.title: Lock and Key Chains: a paper model of why an enzyme cuts only one food
activities.context: In this activity you make three paper food chains with different joins, and three card enzymes with different shapes. You try every enzyme on every chain. The model shows why amylase cuts starch but not fibre.

materials.item: 3 paper strips of different colours, each about 3 centimetres wide and 24 centimetres long
3 pieces of thin card, each about 5 centimetres square, from a cereal box or an old folder
scissors, used by a grown-up, a pencil and a ruler
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the small shapes with the scissors.
activities.record: Rule a table with the three enzymes down the side and the three chains across the top. Write 'cuts' or 'does not fit' in each of the nine boxes.

setup.art: Three paper strips in red, blue and green, each divided into four equal units by pencil lines, with a different small shape cut from the edge at each line: a triangle, a half circle and a square.
setup.caption: 1. Mark each strip into 4 units. Cut one kind of notch at each join: triangle, half circle or square.

setup.art: Three card tags, each with a small tooth at one end shaped like a triangle, a half circle or a square, labelled amylase, pepsin and microbe enzyme.
setup.caption: 2. Make three card enzymes. Each one has a tooth with its own shape.

setup.art: A child fitting the triangle tooth of a card tag into a triangle notch on a red strip, while the half circle tag lies unused beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Try every enzyme on every chain. An enzyme can cut only where its tooth fits.

flow.do: 1. Show a red strip, a blue strip and a green strip. 2. Say that the red one is starch, the blue one is protein and the green one is fibre. 3. Ask your child how an enzyme could find the right chain.
flow.say: Each strip is a long chain of food units. The joins between the units are different shapes.
flow.kid: Look at the three strips. Their joins have different shapes.

ask.q: How could an enzyme tell one chain from another?
good: By the shape of its join.
Like a key that fits one lock.
Only the right shape lets it hold on.

flow.parent: Do not correct the answer. The model will show the idea of a fit.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lock and Key Chains. You meet the three paper food chains and ask how an enzyme could tell them apart.

flow.do: 1. Mark each strip into four units of 6 centimetres. 2. At each of the three joins on a strip, cut a small notch from the edge: a triangle on the red strip, a half circle on the blue strip and a square on the green strip. 3. Cut three card tags with a small tooth at one end. 4. Shape the teeth to match a triangle, a half circle and a square. 5. Label the tags on the back: amylase (triangle tooth), pepsin (half circle tooth) and microbe enzyme (square tooth).
flow.say: The red strip is starch with triangle joins. The blue strip is protein with half-circle joins. The green strip is fibre with square joins. The tags are enzymes. Which tag should fit which strip?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the notches and the tags. The tags are amylase, pepsin and a microbe enzyme.
flow.parent: The teeth must be about 5 millimetres across, so they fit the notches neatly. The microbe enzyme has the square tooth, because only gut microbes make an enzyme for the joins in fibre.
flow.context: In this step of Lock and Key Chains, a grown-up cuts the notches in three food chains and the teeth on three card enzymes.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to try every tag on every strip. 2. When a tooth fits a notch, fold the strip there and tear it, to show a cut. 3. Write 'cuts' or 'does not fit' in the table for each of the nine pairs.
flow.say: Try amylase on all three strips. Then try pepsin and the microbe enzyme. Tear the strip only where a tooth really fits. Write each result down.
flow.kid: Try each tag on each strip. Tear the strip where a tooth fits. Fill in the table.

check.q: In Lock and Key Chains, why can amylase cut the red strip but not the green strip?
options: Its tooth fits only the triangle notch
The green strip is too thick
Amylase is too tired to cut
check.why: An enzyme fits one shape of join and no other. In your food, the starch and the fibre are both made of sugar units, but their joins are different. If you chose 'too thick', try the square tooth on the green strip.

flow.context: In this step of Lock and Key Chains, you try each card enzyme on each paper chain and record which ones cut.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to bend the amylase tooth with a finger and try it on the red strip again. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Ask what the model gets wrong.
flow.say: Bend the amylase tooth, as heat bends an enzyme's shape. Try it on the red strip again. Then say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Bend the amylase tooth. Try the red strip again. Say what you saw and why.

ask.q: What does the bent tooth stand for?
good: An enzyme after it has been heated.
A changed shape that no longer fits.
The saliva that was heated in the Run Test.

flow.parent: The bent tooth stands for heat, or strong acid. A bent enzyme cannot hold its food molecule. This is what happened to the heated saliva in the Run Test, where cup C stayed thick. The model is flat and stiff, and a real enzyme is a small, folded 3D shape. A real enzyme is also used again and again, and the card tag is too.
flow.think: What would a strip need to look like for the bent tag to fit it?
flow.context: This is the last step of Lock and Key Chains. You bend an enzyme and say why the model works and where it fails.

projects.title: The Milk Survey: how many people say that milk gives them trouble?
projects.context: In this three-day project you find out how many people get trouble from milk. You ask about ten people the same short questions about milk and curd. Then you tally the answers and compare them with what scientists found when they tested people in India.

materials.item: a notebook with a page ruled in columns, and a pencil
10 or more family members, neighbours or friends who agree to answer, of different ages
coloured pencils and a ruler, for the bar chart

schedule.what: Write the four questions and your guess for each. Practise on one person at home.
Ask at least ten people. Make a tally mark for each answer. Do not write their names.
Add up the tallies, draw a bar chart and write what you found and what it cannot tell you.

projects.record: A page of tallies, a bar chart of four bars and a short report. It ends with one sentence on what the survey cannot show.

setup.art: A notebook page with four questions written in a row and a grid of empty boxes below them.
setup.caption: 1. Write four questions and a grid for the tally. Add your guess for each question.

setup.art: A child sitting beside an elderly man on a verandah with a notebook, making a tally mark.
setup.caption: 2. Ask ten people the questions. Make a tally mark for each answer.

setup.art: A bar chart with four bars drawn in coloured pencil, one for each question, and a sentence written below it.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar for each question. Write what you found.

flow.do: 1. Day 1. Write these four questions. A: A large tumbler of milk, about 250 millilitres. Does it often give you gas or a stomach ache? B: A small cup of milk, about 100 millilitres. C: Curd or buttermilk. D: Hard cheese or paneer. 2. Answer yes, sometimes or no for each. 3. Write your guess for how many people will say yes to A. 4. Try it on one person at home.
flow.say: We will ask four questions about milk, curd and paneer. First we guess, then we ask.
flow.kid: Write four questions about milk, curd and paneer. Write your guess for the big tumbler. Try it on one person.

ask.q: How many of ten grown-ups do you think will say that a big tumbler of milk gives them trouble?
good: Maybe two or three, because most people drink milk.
Maybe half, because I know several people who avoid it.
I do not know. That is why we ask.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Say the questions aloud and let your child practise on you. Keep the wording the same for every person. Tell people that you are not diagnosing anything, only counting.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Milk Survey. You write four questions and a guess, and practise on one person at home.

flow.do: 1. Day 2. Ask at least 10 people the four questions. 2. Include at least 4 people over 40 years old and at least 3 children. 3. Make a tally mark for each answer on your grid. 4. Add each person's age group, but not their name.
flow.say: Ask each person the same four questions in the same words. Make a tally mark for each answer. Ask a few older people and a few children.
flow.kid: Ask ten people your four questions. Make a tally mark for each answer. Do not write names.
flow.parent: People may tell stories, which is fine, but keep the tally to the three answers. Someone who says milk bothers them should not be told they are ill. Many people have little lactase and live well. A stomach ache that keeps coming back is a matter for a doctor.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Milk Survey. You ask at least ten people the four questions and make tallies.

flow.do: 1. Day 3. Add up the yes answers for each question. 2. Make a bar chart with four bars: draw it, or stack coins for each yes answer. 3. Compare the older people with the children. 4. Write what you found, and what the survey cannot show.
flow.say: Count the yes answers for each question. Make a bar for each one. Does milk trouble more people than curd?
flow.kid: Add up the yes answers. Make four bars. Compare milk, curd and paneer.

ask.q: Which question had the most yes answers, and which had the fewest?
good: The big tumbler of milk had the most.
Curd or buttermilk had the fewest.
Paneer and cheese had few.

ask.q: What can this survey not show?
good: It is only about ten people, so it is too small to be sure.
People may not know why they feel unwell.
A real test measures lactase, and we only asked.

flow.parent: The usual result is that the large tumbler gets more yes answers than the small cup, and curd and paneer get the fewest. That fits the idea that lactose is the cause, since curd and paneer hold less lactose than milk. A survey of ten cannot match the study by Rakesh Tandon and his team in 1981, which tested people in a laboratory. Tell your child that doing a small survey first and asking a bigger question later is how many studies begin.
flow.think: If you asked a hundred people, which of your four bars would you expect to change most?

check.q: In the Milk Survey, why is it important to ask every person the same questions in the same words?
options: So the answers can be counted and compared
So that people finish sooner
So that everyone gives the same answer
check.why: If the wording changes, people may answer different questions, and the tallies would not mean one thing. If you chose 'the same answer', remember that the survey is meant to find out whether the answers differ.

flow.context: This is day 3 of the Milk Survey. You add up the tallies, draw a bar chart and say what the survey can and cannot show.

challenges.title: Make It Faster: speed up the enzyme in saliva
challenges.context: In the Run Test, the saliva in cup B turned thick starch paste runny in 10 minutes. This is a design challenge. You find one change that makes the enzyme in saliva work faster, and you prove it with a fair test.
challenges.problem: Find one change that makes saliva thin the starch paste in less than 10 minutes. Test your change against a control cup. Use the plate race from the Run Test to measure the result.
constraints: Change only one thing at a time.
Every cup gets the same paste, 1 tablespoon.
The test cup has a control cup with the same saliva and no change.
Test each cup after the same waiting time, and measure with the plate race.
Nothing may be heated above what your hand can hold comfortably.
materials: 4 tablespoons of cool starch paste, as made for the Run Test
saliva collected by each child for their own test
a bowl of warm tap water, about the warmth of a bath for a baby
a bowl of cool tap water with a few ice cubes
a large plate leaned on books, a ruler and a timer
general: Change the warmth. Stand one cup in a bowl of warm tap water, and stand the control at room warmth. The enzyme works fastest at about body warmth.
Change the amount of saliva. Use twice as much saliva in one cup and the usual amount in the control.
Change the stirring. Stir one cup 20 times and the control twice. Fresh saliva then meets fresh starch more often.
creative: Cut the starch smaller first. Mash a spoon of cooked rice, and compare it with a lump of cooked rice of the same weight in a second cup.
Try a slice of cooked potato against a spoon of cornflour paste, to see whether the enzyme prefers one starch.
Test the cold side. Stand a cup in iced water, and write how much slower the enzyme becomes.
challenges.your_turn: Choose one change that nobody above has tried. Write your question and what you think will happen and why. Design the test, with a control, and run it. Say what you found and what you would test next.

setup.art: Three steel cups in a row, one standing in a bowl of warm water, one in a bowl of iced water and one on the table, each with a spoon.
setup.caption: 1. Set up a cup for the change you want to test and a control cup with the same paste and saliva.

setup.art: A child stirring each cup in turn and watching a timer, with a notebook showing what each cup got.
setup.caption: 2. Wait the same time for every cup. Then race the blobs on the tilted plate.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of cups and distances, and a line drawn under the cup that ran farthest.
setup.caption: 3. Measure each trail. Say whether your change made a difference.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem. 2. Ask your child to choose one thing to change and to say why it should help. 3. Write the question, the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Which one thing will you change to make the enzyme work faster? You could try warmer water, more saliva or more stirring. Why do you think it will help?
flow.kid: Choose one thing to change. Say why it will help.

ask.q: What will your control cup be?
good: The same paste and saliva with nothing changed.
A cup with the usual amount at room warmth.
The cup that tells me what happens with no change.

flow.parent: A child often wants to change two things at once, such as warm and more saliva. Help them keep it to one. It is the only way to know which one did the work.
flow.context: This is the first step of Make It Faster. You choose one change, say why it should work and name your control.

flow.do: 1. Rinse your mouth and collect about 1 teaspoon of saliva. 2. Put 1 tablespoon of paste in each cup. 3. Add the same saliva to the test cup and the control cup. 4. Make your one change to the test cup. 5. Stir and wait 10 minutes.
flow.say: Both cups get the same paste and the same saliva. Only one thing differs. Stir both and note the time.
flow.kid: Make a test cup and a control cup. Change one thing in the test cup. Wait ten minutes.
flow.parent: The warmth of bath water is about 37 to 40 degrees Celsius and is safe. Do not use hot water, since heat above about 50 degrees stops the enzyme for good, as the heated saliva did in the Run Test.

check.q: In Make It Faster, why must the control cup have the same saliva and the same waiting time?
options: So the one change is the only difference
So both cups finish at once
So that the paste is used up
check.why: A fair test changes one thing. If the control also changed, you could not tell what caused any difference. If you chose 'finish at once', ask what you would then be comparing.

flow.context: In this step of Make It Faster, you set up a test cup and a control cup, and you change one thing in the test cup.

flow.do: 1. Put half a teaspoon from each cup near the top edge of the flat plate. 2. Lift the edge onto the books. 3. After 1 minute, measure each trail. 4. Write whether your change made a difference, and by how much.
flow.say: Race the two blobs down the plate. Did your change make the paste run farther than the control? By how many centimetres? What does that tell you about the enzyme?
flow.kid: Race the two blobs down the plate. Measure each trail. Did your change help?
flow.parent: A difference of about 2 centimetres may be chance. Repeat the test if the gap is small. If the control ran farther, that is a real result too, and the enzyme may not like your change.
flow.think: What would you test next, now that you know the answer?
flow.context: This is the last step of Make It Faster. You race the test cup against the control and say what your change did.

worksheets.title: The food tube, the teeth and the juices (core)

items.p: Which list gives the parts of the food tube in the right order?
opts: Mouth, food pipe, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
Mouth, stomach, food pipe, large intestine, small intestine
Food pipe, mouth, small intestine, stomach, large intestine
Mouth, small intestine, stomach, food pipe, large intestine
items.why: Food goes from the mouth down the food pipe to the stomach. Then it passes through the small intestine, which is long and narrow, and on to the large intestine.

items.p: Put these in the order that food passes through them.
a: Mouth
Food pipe
Stomach
Small intestine
Large intestine
items.why: The mouth breaks the food up. The food pipe squeezes it down. The stomach churns it, the small intestine digests and absorbs it, and the large intestine takes back water.

items.p: A grown-up has ____ teeth in all, if all the wisdom teeth have come in.
items.why: One quarter of the mouth has 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars. That is 8 teeth, and four quarters make 32.

items.p: Label the three layers of a tooth, from the outside to the middle.
a: Enamel: the hard white layer outside, with no living cells
Dentine: the hard yellowish layer under the enamel
Pulp: the soft centre with nerves and blood vessels
items.why: The enamel is on the outside and the pulp is in the centre. The dentine lies between them. A cavity hurts when it reaches the dentine and the nerves in the pulp.
items.art: A blank tooth cut in half from top to bottom, with three blank label lines pointing to the outer layer, the middle layer and the centre.

items.p: Match each tooth to its job.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The front teeth are thin and sharp for cutting. The pointed canines grip and tear. The broad teeth at the back crush and grind.

items.p: A chip in the enamel of a tooth can heal by itself.
items.why: False. Enamel has no living cells, so the body cannot mend it. This is why brushing and avoiding acid matter.

items.p: What does the enzyme in saliva do to starch?
items.why: The enzyme in saliva is amylase. It cuts the long chains of starch into short pieces of sugar. That is why chewed rice begins to taste sweet.

items.p: Sort each food molecule by the place where it is first cut.
items.a: see items
items.why: Starch is first cut by amylase in saliva. Protein is first cut by pepsin in the stomach. Fat waits for bile and lipase in the small intestine.

items.p: Put an enzyme's steps in order, from the first to the last.
items: The enzyme lets the two pieces go
The right food molecule fits the pocket
The enzyme cuts the molecule at one join
The enzyme is free to cut another molecule
a: The right food molecule fits the pocket
The enzyme cuts the molecule at one join
The enzyme lets the two pieces go
The enzyme is free to cut another molecule
items.why: An enzyme has a pocket of one shape. The right molecule fits, and the enzyme cuts it. The enzyme is not changed, so it goes on to cut again.

items.p: An enzyme that cuts protein is called a ____.
a: protease
items.why: Pepsin in the stomach is a protease. An enzyme that cuts starch is an amylase, and an enzyme that cuts fat is a lipase.

items.p: Bile is an enzyme that cuts fat molecules.
items.why: False. Bile breaks fat into tiny droplets and cuts no molecules. Lipase, an enzyme from the pancreas, does the cutting.

items.p: Where does most digested food pass into the blood?
items.why: The small intestine is lined with villi, which give it a huge surface. Digested food passes through them into the blood.

items.p: Why is a well-chewed bite easier to digest than a whole lump?
items.a: Chewing breaks food into small pieces, which have far more outside surface. Saliva and other enzymes can work only on the outside of a piece, so more surface means faster cutting.
items.why: A strong answer says that enzymes work on the outside of the food and that small pieces have more outside. It may mention the sugar lumps in Whole or Crushed.

items.p: Draw one villus. Show a digested sugar crossing into the blood and the way it travels on.
items.a: A finger-shaped bump with a thin wall. A fine blood vessel runs up the middle of it. An arrow shows sugar crossing the wall into the vessel, then a long arrow to the liver, the heart and a muscle.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the wall that the sugar crosses and the blood vessel inside the villus. It then follows the blood to the liver, the heart and the cells.
items.art: A blank page with a faint outline of a finger-shaped bump drawn near the top.

items.p: How many times should a mouthful be chewed?

views.says: Chew every mouthful until it is liquid, whatever the food.
Chew until the food is soft and there are no hard lumps. A banana needs few chews.

views.who: A cook of thick soft porridge
views.says: A few chews are enough. The cooking has already done much of the work.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you know about enzymes and surface. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. The strongest answers say that chewing gives enzymes more surface, and that the right number depends on the food.
items.why: Each view has something right. A strong answer links the number of chews to the food and to the surface that the enzymes can reach.

items.p: Sort each habit: good for the teeth, or bad for the teeth?
items: rinsing with water after a meal
visiting a dentist when a tooth hurts
going to bed with food stuck on the teeth
items.a: see items
items.why: Mouth bacteria make acid from sugar, and acid dissolves enamel that cannot grow back. Brushing, rinsing and fewer sweets keep the acid low.

items.p: The liver, the biggest gland in the body, lies on the ____ side of the stomach.
a: right
items.why: The liver sits on the right side, under the lower ribs. It makes bile for the small intestine.

worksheets.title: Why each station works as it does (stretch)

items.p: Why does the enzyme in saliva stop working in the stomach?
opts: The acid changes the shape of the enzyme
The stomach is too cold for it
There is no starch in the stomach
The enzyme runs out of saliva
items.why: An enzyme works only while its shape fits its food. Strong acid changes that shape, so amylase stops. Pepsin works only in acid.

items.p: A tablet cancels the acid in a stomach. What happens to the pepsin there?
opts: It stops working, because it needs acid
It works faster, because the acid is gone
items.why: Pepsin is switched on by acid, and it works only in acid. If the acid is cancelled, protein digestion in the stomach slows down.

items.p: Label the three stations on this strip of the food tube with the right acidity.
a: Mouth: about pH 7, amylase works here
Stomach: about pH 2, pepsin works here
Small intestine: about pH 7, the enzymes of the pancreas work here
items.why: The mouth and small intestine are close to neutral. The stomach is strongly acid. Each station keeps the acidity that suits its enzymes.
items.art: A long horizontal strip split into three coloured zones, with a blank line above each zone.

items.p: Put the steps for a bite of boiled potato in order.
items: Amylase from the pancreas finishes the cutting
Acid in the stomach stops the amylase from saliva
Amylase in saliva starts to cut the starch
Glucose crosses a villus into the blood
a: Amylase in saliva starts to cut the starch
Acid in the stomach stops the amylase from saliva
Amylase from the pancreas finishes the cutting
Glucose crosses a villus into the blood
items.why: Potato is rich in starch, which is cut in two rounds, first in the mouth and then in the small intestine. In between, the stomach acid stops the first enzyme.

items.p: Food and drink bring 2 litres of water into the tube. Juices add 7 litres. How many litres enter in all?
items.why: Add the water taken in and the juices added. 2 + 7 = 9 litres. Nearly all of it is taken back, and only about 100 millilitres leave.

items.p: In a Run Test, cup A ran 2 centimetres and cup B ran 16. How many centimetres farther did cup B run?
items.why: Subtract the control from the saliva cup. 16 - 2 = 14 centimetres farther. The control shows what the paste does with no saliva.

items.p: Is each job done by force, or by cutting molecules with an enzyme?
items: the squeezing of the intestine wall
items.a: see items
items.why: Chewing, churning and squeezing break food into smaller lumps, but the lumps are still the same molecules. Only enzymes cut the molecules themselves.

items.p: Lipase cuts fat. Why does the body also need bile?
opts: Droplets give lipase much more surface to work on
Bile is a stronger enzyme than lipase
Bile cuts the fat into sugar
items.why: Fat floats in a large blob in watery juice. Bile breaks it into tiny droplets, as dish soap does to grease. Lipase can then reach far more of the fat.

items.p: Match each animal to the part of her gut that is special.
pairs: A large side pouch of microbes
A small large intestine, for easy meat
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each gut fits the food. Plant-eaters house microbes in extra chambers or pouches. A crow grinds food in a muscular gizzard. A cat's large intestine is small because meat is easy to digest.

items.p: Explain why a cow needs microbes to digest grass, but a cat does not need them to digest meat.
items.a: Grass is mostly fibre. No enzyme made by a cow can cut fibre, but microbes in her rumen can. Meat is mostly protein and fat, which the cat's own enzymes cut.
items.why: A strong answer names fibre, says that animals with backbones do not make an enzyme for it, and says that microbes make one. It then says that meat has no such problem.

items.p: Who digests the grass that a cow eats?

views.says: The cow does. She chews, swallows and grows fat on the grass.
The microbes do the cutting. The cow takes in the acids that they make.
The cow and her microbes are one working system. Nothing is digested by one of them alone.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you know about fibre and enzymes. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. A strong answer says that fibre cannot be cut by the cow's own enzymes, so the microbes are needed.
items.why: Each view is partly right. The strongest answers say what each partner does and why the cow could not live on grass without the microbes.

items.p: Someone says gut bacteria are germs, so a body is better without them. Give two reasons this is wrong.
items.a: Gut bacteria cut fibre that we cannot cut, and the cells of the large intestine use the acids they make. They also make vitamin K and take up space, so harmful microbes find it hard to settle.
items.why: A strong answer gives two real jobs. It may add that animals raised without gut microbes need more food to stay the same weight.

items.p: Draw the route of a sugar molecule from a spoon of rice to a muscle in the leg.
items.a: The sugar travels through the mouth, the food pipe, the stomach and the small intestine. It crosses a villus into the blood. The blood goes to the liver, then to the heart, and then to the leg muscle.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the sugar crosses the wall of the small intestine. It then follows the blood through the liver and the heart to the leg.
items.art: A blank outline of a child's body from head to feet with no organs drawn.

items.p: Fibre is useless, because the body cannot cut it with its own enzymes.
items.why: False. Gut bacteria ferment fibre into acids that feed the cells of the large intestine. Fibre also holds water, which keeps the contents of the gut soft and moving.

items.p: Which kind of tooth is missing in a small child's 20 milk teeth?
items.why: A child has 2 incisors, 1 canine and 2 molars in each quarter of the mouth. The premolars come in only with the permanent teeth.

items.p: A friend laughs loudly while eating a chapati and starts to cough. Explain what happened, using the words windpipe and food pipe. Then give one rule for eating that would help.
items.a: Laughing kept the windpipe open, so a bit of chapati went the wrong way, into the windpipe, instead of down the food pipe. The cough pushes it out. A rule: chew small mouthfuls and do not talk or laugh with food in the mouth.
items.why: A strong answer names both tubes and says that the flap over the windpipe could not close fully. The rule should be about small mouthfuls or not talking while eating.

items.p: Rani is 8 and has a heavy stomach after a wedding lunch. Give two things that may have caused it, one thing she can take at home, and two signs that mean she must see a doctor.
items.a: Causes: a very big or oily meal, eating very fast, or food that was left out and turned bad. At home: buttermilk or curd, rest, and ORS if she has loose motions. Doctor: strong or returning pain, vomiting that will not stop, blood in vomit or motion, or being very sleepy with a very dry mouth.
items.why: A strong answer gives real causes, a gentle home step and clear warning signs. Home steps help with mild trouble only.

items.p: You want to know whether more saliva makes starch paste runnier. Which pair of cups is a fair test?
opts: Same paste and time, with 1 drop or 3 drops
Different paste and time, with 1 drop and with 3 drops
Paste with saliva, and a different paste with water
Warm paste with saliva, and cold paste with more saliva
items.why: A fair test changes one thing only. Here it is the amount of saliva, and the paste and time stay the same.

items.p: Many people think that acid does the digesting in the stomach. What test would you do to check this?
items.a: Put the same piece of boiled egg white in three cups. Add stomach-strength acid to one, stomach juice with pepsin to another, and water to the third. Keep them warm for some hours and compare. Acid alone should change the egg white very little.
items.why: A strong answer names a control and one thing that changes between the cups. It says what would show that acid alone does not digest, as Theodor Schwann found in 1836.

items.p: If a cup of saliva and paste stays thick, the saliva must have been heated.
items.why: False. Warm paste, too little saliva, too short a wait or lemon juice could all do it. You can know only by comparing with other cups.

items.p: Is a kitchen part of the human digestive system?

views.says: Yes. Grinding, boiling and fermenting do part of the breaking down before the first bite.
No. A digestive system is made of body parts, and a kitchen is not part of a body.
Our guts became small because cooking did some of their work. So the kitchen shaped the body.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you know about cooked and raw starch. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. A strong answer uses an example such as idli batter, which is ground and fermented before the meal.
items.why: The question is about where to draw a line. A strong answer says what the line depends on, and notes that scientists still argue about when cooking began.

items.p: Isabgol gel stayed thick when saliva was added. What can you conclude?
opts: Saliva did not cut the fibre in the gel
Saliva was too cold to work
The gel was too thick to be cut
items.why: The starch cup next to it ran, so the saliva was working. The gel did not change, so the enzyme in saliva does not fit the joins in this fibre.

items.p: Out of 12 South Indians tested, 8 had low lactase. What fraction is that, in its simplest form?
items.why: 8 out of 12 is 8/12. Divide the top and the bottom by 4 to get 2/3, or two out of three.

items.p: A cup of paste with water in place of saliva, kept to compare with the saliva cups, is called the ____.
a: control
items.why: The control shows what happens with the thing you are testing left out. Without it, you cannot tell what the saliva added.

items.p: Why can many people take curd or buttermilk when a large tumbler of milk gives them a stomach ache?
opts: Curd bacteria have already used up part of the lactose
Curd contains no sugar at all
Curd is digested in the mouth
Curd is made without any milk
items.why: Bacteria in curd eat milk sugar and carry lactase of their own. So less lactose reaches the large intestine, where it would be fermented and make gas.

items.p: Put these in order to show how milk can give a stomach ache.
items: Bacteria in the large intestine ferment the lactose
Little lactase is made, so lactose is not cut
A large tumbler of milk reaches the small intestine
Gas and acids make the belly ache
The uncut lactose passes into the large intestine
a: A large tumbler of milk reaches the small intestine
Little lactase is made, so lactose is not cut
The uncut lactose passes into the large intestine
Bacteria in the large intestine ferment the lactose
Gas and acids make the belly ache
items.why: Lactose can be absorbed only after lactase cuts it. If it is not cut, it passes on, and the bacteria at the end of the tube feed on it.

items.p: Plan a fair test: does saliva at body warmth cut starch faster than saliva at room warmth?
items.a: Make two cups with the same paste and the same saliva. Stand one in a bowl of bath-warm water and leave the other at room warmth. Wait 10 minutes and race both blobs on a tilted plate. Compare how far each ran, and repeat once.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the warmth, keeps the paste, saliva, time and plate the same, and says what would count as a difference.

items.p: Match each claim to the evidence that supports it.
pairs: Schwann in 1836 found that acid of stomach strength changed meat very little
People differ in how much amylase they make
In 2007 a team counted from 2 to 15 copies of the amylase gene
Animals raised with no gut microbes need more food to keep their weight
A cow's rumen holds more than 100 litres
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each claim comes from a finding. Digestion is studied by testing the parts one at a time and measuring what each one does.

items.p: Some people have more copies of the amylase gene, so some people cannot digest starch at all.
items.why: False. Everyone makes some amylase and can digest starch. The people in the study differed in how much, from 2 to 15 copies of the gene.

items.p: Sketch the four bars you expect for the Run Test cups A to D, and label each bar.
items.a: A tall bar for cup B with plain saliva. Short bars, about as short as the water cup, for cup C with heated saliva and cup D with saliva and lemon. A short bar for cup A with water.
items.why: A strong sketch shows the control cup short, the plain saliva cup tall, and the heated and acid cups short. It labels each cup by what went in.
items.art: A blank pair of axes with the label 'How far the blob ran' on the side and the letters A, B, C and D along the bottom.

items.p: A scientist says the appendix is useless, because people live well without it. Which fact weakens this?
opts: It has appeared separately in more than 30 groups of mammals
Some people have had their appendix removed
It is a thin tube about as long as a finger
It is not needed to digest rice
items.why: A part that appears again and again in the history of mammals, and is rarely lost, probably does a job. People who live well without it show only that the job is not essential.

items.p: Cooking bursts starch grains and softens food. Give one reason this could help a body with a small gut.
items.a: Cooked food is easier for enzymes to cut, so less gut length and less chewing are needed to get the same energy from the same food.
items.why: A strong answer links cooking to easier digestion and then to a body that can afford a shorter gut. It may say that scientists still argue about when this began.

quiz.p: Which organ makes acid and pepsin?
quiz.why: The wall of the stomach makes hydrochloric acid and pepsin. The liver makes bile, and the mouth makes saliva.

quiz.p: Which of these cuts starch into sugar?
quiz.why: Amylase cuts starch. Pepsin cuts protein, lipase cuts fat, and bile only breaks fat into droplets.

quiz.p: How many canines does a grown-up have?
quiz.why: There is one canine in each quarter of the mouth, so there are four. The pointed canines grip and tear.

quiz.p: What is the hardest substance in the body?
quiz.why: Enamel is the hardest, and it has no living cells. Dentine and bone are hard but living.

quiz.p: Saliva and a few drops of lemon juice are added to thick starch paste. What do you expect?
opts: The paste stays thick, because acid stops amylase
The paste turns runny, because lemon helps
The paste turns to sugar at once
quiz.why: Lemon juice is acid, like the stomach. Acid changes the shape of amylase, so it cannot cut the starch.

quiz.p: Digestion of protein begins in the mouth.
quiz.why: False. Digestion of protein begins in the stomach, where pepsin works in acid. Starch is the food that begins to be cut in the mouth.

quiz.p: What do the villi in the small intestine do?
opts: Pass digested food into the blood
quiz.why: Villi are tiny finger-shaped bumps. They give the lining a huge surface, and digested food crosses them into the blood.

quiz.p: No human enzyme can cut fibre. What happens to it in the large intestine?
quiz.why: Gut bacteria make enzymes that fit the joins in fibre. They ferment it into acids, which the cells of the large intestine can use.

quiz.p: Put these in order, to show the route of a sugar molecule from a rice grain to a muscle.
a: The blood in a villus
The liver
The heart
A leg muscle
quiz.why: Sugar crosses into the blood in a villus. The blood goes first to the liver, then to the heart, and the heart pumps it to the muscle.

quiz.p: Which part of a rabbit's gut is much bigger than a cat's, and why?
opts: The large intestine and caecum, where microbes cut plant fibre
The food pipe, to swallow bigger pieces
Nothing, a rabbit's gut is the same as a cat's
quiz.why: Plants are rich in fibre, and no enzyme of an animal with a backbone cuts it. Microbes do it slowly, in the large intestine and the caecum. Measurements show that this is where plant-eaters differ most from meat-eaters.

quiz.p: Which cup is a good control for a test of saliva on starch paste?
opts: Paste with water in place of saliva
quiz.why: A control leaves out the thing you test. Paste with water shows what the paste does without saliva.

opts: The enzyme that cuts milk sugar
quiz.why: Lactose is the sugar in milk. Lactase is the enzyme in the small intestine that cuts it in two so that it can be absorbed.

quiz.p: Why should you not talk or laugh with food in your mouth?
opts: The windpipe stays open, so a bit of food can slip into it and make you choke
The enzymes in the mouth stop working
The food would taste of nothing
quiz.why: When you swallow, a flap closes over the windpipe. Laughing keeps it open, and food can go the wrong way. Saliva does not run out when you talk, and enzymes do not mind noise.

quiz.p: Which organ is the biggest gland in the body?
quiz.why: The liver is the biggest gland, and it makes bile. The pancreas is also a gland, but it is much smaller. The stomach and the tongue are not glands.

quiz.p: A child has a stomach upset. Which sign means a grown-up must take her to a doctor?
opts: Vomiting that will not stop, with a very dry mouth
A heavy feeling that is gone in an hour
quiz.why: Vomiting that does not stop, and a very dry mouth, can mean the body is losing too much water. The other signs are mild and usually pass on their own.

quiz.p: Why does it help your teeth to rinse with water after a sweet and to eat fewer sweets?
opts: Bacteria turn sugar into acid that slowly dissolves enamel, and enamel cannot mend itself
Sweets make the teeth grow too many
quiz.why: Sugar feeds mouth bacteria, and they make acid. Enamel has no living cells, so it cannot heal once it dissolves. Less sugar and a quick rinse leave less acid on the teeth.

applications: Lactose-free milk has had lactase added at the dairy, so the milk sugar is already cut. Many shops also sell lactase tablets for people who make little lactase.
Raw papaya and pineapple hold enzymes that cut protein, called papain and bromelain. Cooks in many parts of India have used raw papaya to make tough meat tender.
Sprouted ragi flour holds amylase. Mixed into a thick ragi porridge, it makes the porridge thinner, the way saliva thinned the starch paste. Porridges for small children are often made this way.

Some people make too little pancreatic juice, so their food is not fully digested. Doctors give them capsules of the enzymes that the pancreas should make, and take care that the capsules are not dissolved by stomach acid.
Farmers use a chaff cutter to chop fodder into short pieces. A cow's rumen microbes then have more surface to work on, and the cow wastes less of what she eats.
Dentists tell people to rinse after sweet food, and to use toothpaste with fluoride. Fluoride makes enamel harder to dissolve in the acid made by mouth bacteria.
Antibiotics kill many gut bacteria as well as harmful ones. Doctors give them only when they are needed, and the gut microbes usually recover over some weeks.

open_questions.q: What does the appendix do in people?
open_questions.why_open: One idea is that it keeps a store of helpful bacteria. An appendix has appeared separately more than 30 times in mammals. But nobody has shown clearly what it does in a person.

open_questions.q: How much do gut microbes change a person's mood, weight and health?
open_questions.why_open: In mice raised with no gut microbes, the brain and behaviour grow differently. In people, studies show links, but they rarely show which came first. Scientists are still testing.

open_questions.q: Which mixture of gut microbes is a healthy one?
open_questions.why_open: Healthy people carry very different mixtures, which also change with age and food. Scientists have not found one ideal mixture.

open_questions.q: When did our ancestors start cooking, and how much did it change our guts?
open_questions.why_open: Richard Wrangham thinks cooking began almost 2 million years ago. The oldest fireplaces that everyone accepts are much younger. The question is still open.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of microbes live in the human gut?
open_questions.why_open: Many kinds in one person are counted, and many have never been grown in a laboratory. Scientists know most of them only from their genes.

maths.problem: In a Run Test, the water cup ran 2 centimetres and the saliva cup ran 18 centimetres. How many times as far did the saliva cup run?
maths.explain: Divide the saliva cup by the water cup: 18 ÷ 2 = 9. The saliva cup ran 9 times as far.
maths.context: In the Run Test you race four pastes down a tilted plate and measure how far each runs. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Saying how many times farther is a fairer way to compare than saying how many centimetres farther, since it works for any size of plate.

maths.problem: A cube of rock sugar is 2 centimetres on each side. It has 6 faces, each 2 by 2 centimetres. Cut into eight cubes of 1 centimetre, how many times as much outside surface is there in all?
maths.explain: The big cube has 6 faces of 4 square centimetres, which is 24. Each small cube has 6 faces of 1 square centimetre, which is 6. Eight small cubes have 8 × 6 = 48. And 48 ÷ 24 = 2.
maths.context: In Whole or Crushed, a whole lump, pieces and powder of the same sugar dissolve at very different speeds.
maths.why_maths: The sugar's amount does not change when it is cut, but its outside surface does. That is the number that explains why chewing helps enzymes.

maths.problem: One quarter of a grown-up's mouth holds 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars. A child of 10 has about 24 teeth. How many more teeth can come, up to 32?
maths.explain: A quarter has 2 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 8 teeth. Four quarters have 4 × 8 = 32. And 32 - 24 = 8 more. The last four are the wisdom teeth, which come late, and some people never get them.
maths.context: Your teeth are four kinds, and the mouth is made of four matching quarters.
maths.why_maths: A pattern repeated in four quarters lets you find the whole by multiplying one part, then compare it with a child's count.

maths.problem: In The Gut Ladder, a rabbit of about 3 kilograms has intestines about 340 centimetres long. A cat of about 2.5 kilograms has intestines about 140 centimetres long. Whose intestines are longer, and by how many metres?
maths.explain: The rabbit: 340 centimetres is 3.4 metres. The cat: 140 centimetres is 1.4 metres. And 3.4 - 1.4 = 2 metres more for the rabbit, who weighs only a little more than the cat.
maths.context: In The Gut Ladder, you cut strips to show the measured length of each animal's gut.
maths.why_maths: The rabbit and the cat weigh about the same, so the difference in length is not just size. Subtracting measured lengths compares them fairly.

maths.problem: The body takes in 9 litres of water and juices a day, and only about 100 millilitres leave the body. About how many litres does the body take back, and what fraction of the 9 litres leaves?
maths.answer: About 8.9 litres is taken back. About 1 part in 90 leaves.
maths.explain: 100 millilitres is 0.1 litre. And 9 - 0.1 = 8.9 litres. The fraction that leaves is 0.1 ÷ 9, about 1 ÷ 90.
maths.context: The gut takes in water with food and drink, and its own juices add more. Almost all of it is taken back in the small and large intestines.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how complete the taking back is. Saying that about 99 parts in 100 are saved is a clear way to say it.

maths.problem: About two in three South Indians and one in four North Indians tested had low lactase. In a group of 12 people from each region, how many would you expect to have low lactase in each group? How much do the two numbers differ?
maths.answer: 8 in the South group and 3 in the North group, which differ by 5.
maths.explain: Two thirds of 12 is 12 ÷ 3 × 2 = 8. A quarter of 12 is 12 ÷ 4 = 3. And 8 - 3 = 5.
maths.context: In 1981, Rakesh Tandon and his team tested healthy grown-ups in India and found that low lactase was more common in the South than in the North.
maths.why_maths: Taking a fraction of a small group shows what a study's percentages mean for a real group of people, and how big the gap between two regions is.

maths.problem: The lining of a grown-up's small intestine has a surface of about 30 square metres. A room is 6 metres long and 5 metres wide. How does its floor compare with that surface?
maths.answer: The floor is also 30 square metres. They are about the same.
maths.explain: The floor is 6 × 5 = 30 square metres. So the folded lining of the small intestine has about as much surface as the floor of one room.
maths.context: The small intestine is only 3 to 6 metres long, but its folds and villi give its lining a huge surface for absorbing food.
maths.why_maths: Turning a surface into the floor of a room makes the number easy to picture and shows why folds and villi matter.

Why does amylase stop working in the stomach?
warmup.a: The strong acid changes its shape, so it can no longer hold starch.

warmup.q: What does pepsin need to work?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that enzymes can work with no living cell at all? This card tells the true story of a juice made from yeast.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1850s and 1860s, the French scientist Louis Pasteur showed that yeast turn sugar into alcohol. Many scientists then held that only a living cell could cause such a change. In 1877 the German scientist Wilhelm Kühne named the substances that do the work 'enzymes', from Greek words meaning 'in yeast'. But nobody had shown one working with no living cell. In 1897 the German chemist Eduard Buchner ground yeast with sand and pressed out a juice. The juice held no living yeast cells. He stirred in a great deal of sugar. The juice began to bubble. The sugar was turning into alcohol and gas. A juice with no living cell could still do the work. Buchner won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1907. In 1913 Maud Menten, a doctor from Canada, and Leonor Michaelis measured how fast an enzyme from yeast works, and the rule still carries both names. In 1926 James Sumner made crystals of one enzyme and showed that it is a protein.
how_we_found_out.who: Louis Pasteur, Wilhelm Kühne, Eduard Buchner, Maud Menten with Leonor Michaelis, and James Sumner
how_we_found_out.when: Pasteur in the 1850s and 1860s, the name 'enzyme' in 1877, Buchner's pressed juice in 1897, Menten and Michaelis's measurements in 1913, and Sumner's crystals in 1926
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the work of digesting and fermenting can be done only by a living cell. Buchner showed that a juice with no living cells could still turn sugar into alcohol and gas.
how_we_found_out.art: A laboratory bench in 1897 with a heavy press, a bowl of pale yeast, a glass flask of bubbling juice and a man in a dark coat writing in a notebook.

roots.context: In this lesson you found out that each enzyme cuts one kind of molecule, and that gut microbes cut the fibre that you cannot. Here we ask what this tells us about food and about the one who eats it.

deep_truth.truth: In Starch or Fibre, saliva made the starch paste runny and left the fibre gel thick. Both are chains of sugar units, and an enzyme cuts only the joins it fits. We have no enzyme for the joins in fibre, but gut microbes have. So whether a plant counts as food depends on the enzymes the eater has or can borrow from microbes.
deep_truth.habit: We talk about food as if being food were a property of the thing itself, like its colour. But grass is food for a cow and her microbes together, and it is not food for a person alone. Whether something is food depends on whether the eater has the right enzymes for it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Run Test and Starch or Fibre, saliva cut one chain of sugar units and left the other. In Lock and Key Chains, only the tooth of the right shape fitted a notch in the strip. In Right Juice, Right Place, the fibre cards ended up with the gut bacteria. In a cow's rumen, the microbes have a great deal of room, and they cut the fibre in grass. That is what makes grass food for her.

three.who_am_i: You carry about as many bacteria in your gut as you have human cells in your body. Some of the food you live on is cut by those bacteria, and not by you.
three.what_is_life: Every animal takes food apart with enzymes, and each enzyme cuts one kind of join. Many animals, including us, share this work with microbes.
three.what_is_this_world: The same sugar units join into starch in a potato, and they join in a different way into fibre in a leaf. Whether a meal counts as food depends on who is eating it.

roots.thread: A leaf is made of chains of sugar, which the plant builds from sunlight, water and air. A cow cannot cut some of those chains, but her microbes can. The cow gives the microbes a warm, wet home and a steady supply of grass. The microbes give the cow acids that she lives on. Neither partner could live on grass alone. In your own large intestine, the same kind of arrangement works on a smaller scale.

teachings.teaching: The text says that the divine becomes the fire of digestion, called vaishvanara, in the body of every living being. With the breath it digests the four kinds of food.
teachings.link: Many traditions saw digestion as a kind of fire, which turns food into the stuff of life. Today we see that the work is done by enzymes, at body warmth and in the right acidity, and not by a flame. Both pictures say that digesting is more than breaking food into lumps.

teachings.teaching: This old text on medicine treats the body's digestive fire, called agni, as the root of health. It says that health depends on digesting well.
teachings.link: The text teaches that each person digests in their own way. Your own tests showed that two people can differ in amylase and lactase. The text gives a teaching about health. It does not describe enzymes, which were found much later.

science.text: The mitochondria in your cells came from bacteria that began to live inside a larger cell, more than a billion years ago. Lynn Margulis argued this in 1967, and it is now widely accepted.
How much your gut microbes shape your weight, your mood and your health is still being studied. Many studies show links, and few show which one causes which.

other_view.view: A body and its microbes are separate living beings who cooperate. Animals raised with no gut microbes survive in clean laboratories with extra food. So the microbes are partners, not parts of the body. Whether the pair should count as one unit is still argued.

practice.title: One slow bite
practice.say: Take a small piece of plain roti or a spoon of plain rice. Put it in your mouth and chew it slowly for 30 seconds. Notice how your mouth fills with saliva. Notice whether the taste changes. Swallow, and feel the food go down. Breathe quietly three times.

ask: Is grass food? Or does it become food only when a cow and her microbes eat it?
A cow cannot digest grass without her microbes. Where does the cow end and her microbes begin?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was reasoned through step by step, as a parent and child would do it in a city flat. None of them has been tried at home yet, so treat the expected results as likely, not certain. The Run Test (core) needs cornflour, a stove, a steel plate and 2 or 3 books. The cooked paste must be cool and as thick as custard. Cup B usually runs far, and the other three stay thick. If nothing runs, the paste was probably still warm. The saliva cups need about a quarter teaspoon of saliva each. Collecting it takes two or three minutes, and the lemon wedge helps. Starch or Fibre (core) needs isabgol husk, or slimy bhindi water. A gel that is too runny gets another half teaspoon of husk. Listen to a Gut needs a quiet room. Counts differ from person to person, and two people are too few to settle the question, as the step says. Mouth Waters (core) is a short activity and its result varies. Whole or Crushed (core) needs kalkandu, or big crystals of ordinary sugar. A whole lump can take 4 minutes or more to vanish, so the step says to stop at 8 minutes. The Gut Ladder needs about 7 metres of newspaper or string. Lock and Key Chains needs card and scissors, and a grown-up cuts the small shapes. The Milk Survey takes three short days and needs ten people willing to answer. Make It Faster needs the paste from the Run Test, and it is open on purpose, since the child chooses what to change. Right Juice, Right Place has 20 cards and a mat of five spaces, so the best score alone is 40. Whose Teeth, Whose Gut? has 12 cards, so the best score alone is 36. Nothing needs a garden or an animal. Take care with the lactose results. A stomach ache that keeps coming back needs a doctor, and the unit says so where it matters.
